label: thm: theta is continuous-INTRO
title: \protect\theoremname
body_md:
\label{thm: theta is continuous-INTRO}  The optimal test function
$\Theta_{P}$ can extend to a concave function on the whole space.
In particular, $\Theta_{P}$ is continuous up to the boundary of $P$,
and the subdifferential set $\partial\left(-\Theta_{P}\right)\left(\mathrm{int}P\right)$
is bounded.

label: thm: Chow-desta INTRO
title: \protect\theoremname
body_md:
\label{thm: Chow-desta INTRO}

For toric variety $(X,L)$ given by lattice polytope $P\subset M_{\mathbb{R}}$,
suppose that $\iota_{k}:X\hookrightarrow\mathbb{P}R^{*}_{k}$ is an
embedding ($k\ge n-1$ is enough). 

(1) Subvariety $\iota_{k}(X)\subset\mathbb{P}R^{*}_{k}$ is Chow-semistable
(w.r.t. the action of $\mathrm{SL}(R_{k})$) if and only if the constant
vector $\left|P_{k}\right|^{-1}\in\Sigma(P_{k})$, or equivalently
$\sigma_{k}\equiv\left|P_{k}\right|^{-1}$. 

(2) When $\iota_{k}(X)$ is Chow-unstable, the minimizers (i.e. maximal
Chow-destabilizers) of 
\begin{equation}
\inf\left\{ \frac{M_{k}(\chi)}{\left\Vert \chi\right\Vert _{2}}\ \Big|\ \chi\in\mathcal{N}(R_{k})\backslash\{\chi_{tr}\}\right\} \label{eq: min Chow  INTRO}
\end{equation}
 are of the form $a\chi^{*}_{k}$ ($a>0$), where $\chi^{*}_{k}$
is diagonalized by the basis $\left\{ s_{u,k}\right\} _{u\in P_{k}}$
(\ref{eq:eigen basis}) and satisfies 
\[
\chi^{*}_{k}(s_{u,k})=\left|P_{k}\right|^{-1}-\sigma_{k}(u),\ \forall u\in P_{k}.
\]

title: \protect\theoremname
body_md:
For any marked polytope $(Q,A)$ with shortest GKZ vector $\sigma_{A}\in\Sigma(A)$,
we have 

(1) $\sigma_{A}$ is convex, that means the restriction of the convex
envelope $\sigma^{\vee}_{A}|_{A}=\sigma_{A}$. 

(2) $\sigma_{A}:A\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is positive at each point.

label: thm:main converge
title: \protect\theoremname
body_md:
\label{thm:main converge} (1) When $P$ is a Delzant lattice polytope,
the quantum minimizer $\psi_{k}$ (\ref{eq:quantum mini INTRO}) converges
to $-\Theta_{P}$ in $L^{2}(P)$ and uniformly on every compact set
$K\subset\mathrm{int}P$. In particular, at any point $x\in\mathrm{int}P$,
we have 
\begin{equation}
V_{P}k^{n}\sigma^{\vee}_{k}(x)=1-\frac{\Theta_{P}(x)}{2k}+\mathrm{o}\left(\frac{1}{k}\right).
\end{equation}
Moreover, we have 
\[
\min\Psi_{k}\rightarrow\min\Psi,\ \lim_{k}\mathbb{M}^{\mathrm{rel}}_{P}(\psi_{k})=\mathbb{M}^{\mathrm{rel}}_{P}(-\Theta_{P})=-\left\Vert \Theta_{P}-\ell_{P}\right\Vert ^{2}_{L^{2}}.
\]

(2) For a general lattice polytope $P$, $\psi_{k}$ uniformly converges
to $-\Theta_{P}$ over $P$ if and only if $\{\psi_{k}\}$ is $C^{0}$-precompact,
i.e., uniformly bounded and equicontinuous.
head: environment

title: \protect\corollaryname
body_md:
If $P$ is a relatively K-unstable Delzant polytope (i.e. $\Theta_{P}\neq\ell_{P}$),
then $\mathbb{M}^{\mathrm{rel}}_{P}(\sigma^{\vee}_{k})<0$ for sufficiently
large $k$.

title: \protect\propositionname
body_md:
A NA norm $\chi$ on $R_{k}$ is $T_{\mathbb{C}}$-invariant if and only
if $\chi$ is diagonalized by the eigen-sections $\left\{ s_{u,k}\mid u\in P_{k}\right\} $.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For any $\chi\in\mathcal{N}(R_{k})^{T}$, the associated filtration
$F^{\lambda}=\left\{ s\in R_{k}\mid\chi(s)\geq\lambda\right\} $ is
$T_{\mathbb{C}}$-invariant for any $\lambda$. Since $R_{k}$ is multiplicity-free,
$F^{\lambda}$ is spanned by some $s_{u,k}$. This implies that $\chi$
is diagonalized by $(s_{u,k})$. The converse direction is trivial.
head: environment

title: \protect\remarkname
body_md:
Although $\mathbb{T}^{\mathrm{an}}$ has no usual group structure, one can
define a multi-valued product and an action on $X^{\mathrm{an}}$, refer to
\cite[§4.2]{burgos_gil_arithmetic_2014}. The NA compact torus $\mathbb{S}^{\mathrm{an}}\subset\mathbb{T}^{\mathrm{an}}$
is the subset of semivaluations such that $v(\mathsf{x}^{m})=0$ for
all $m\in M$. Then the tropicalization $N_{P}$ is the quotient space
of $X^{\mathrm{an}}$ modulo the action of $\mathbb{S}^{\mathrm{an}}$. In the Archimedean
setting, $N_{P}$ is the quotient space of $X(\mathbb{C})$ modulo the action
of $T_{\mathbb{R}}$. So in both settings, $N_{P}$ is the common stage
for toric reduction.

head: environment

title: \protect\definitionname
body_md:
Let $(X,L)$ be the toric variety associated to a lattice polytope
$P\subset M_{\mathbb{R}}$. 

(1) For any $U\subset N_{P}$, function $\varphi:\varrho^{-1}(U)\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$
is \textit{torus-invariant} if $\mathscr{R}^{*}\varphi=\varphi$, i.e.
$\varphi$ is constant along the fibers of tropicalization map. Let
$\mathrm{PSH}^{{\scriptscriptstyle \mathsf{NA}}}_{T}(L)$ ($\mathrm{CPSH}^{{\scriptscriptstyle \mathsf{NA}}}_{T}(L)$) be the
space of torus-invariant (continuous) psh metrics on $L^{\mathrm{an}}$. 

(2) For a torus-invariant metric $\varphi$ on $L^{\mathrm{an}}$, its tropical
potential $F_{\varphi}:N_{\mathbb{R}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is defined
as 
\begin{equation}
F_{\varphi}(y)\coloneqq-\log\left|s_{D}\right|_{\varphi}(\vartheta_{y})=\vartheta_{y}(s_{D})+\varphi(\vartheta_{y})=F_{P}(y)+\varphi(\vartheta_{y}).\label{eq:def of trop poten}
\end{equation}
The last $=$ is due to Proposition \ref{prop: trop of FS} (1) below,
and $F_{P}(y)\coloneqq\max_{u\in P}\left\langle u,y\right\rangle $
is the support function of $P$.
head: environment

label: prop: trop of FS
title: \protect\propositionname
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) Take a full-dimensional cone $\sigma\in\mathcal{F}_{P}$ containing
$-y$. Let $m_{\sigma}$ be the corresponding vertex of $P$, then
we have $\left\langle m_{\sigma},y\right\rangle =\max_{u\in P}\left\langle u,y\right\rangle =F_{P}(y)$.
Note that $X_{\sigma}$ contains the center of valuation $\vartheta_{y}$,
and $s_{\sigma}\coloneqq\mathsf{x}^{m_{\sigma}}s_{D}$ (\ref{eq:frame})
is a frame of $L$ over $X_{\sigma}$. We represent $s_{D}=\mathsf{x}^{-m_{\sigma}}s_{\sigma}$.
By the definition of $\vartheta_{y}(s_{D})$, we have 
\[
\vartheta_{y}(s_{D})=\vartheta_{y}(\mathsf{x}^{-m_{\sigma}})=\left\langle m_{\sigma},y\right\rangle =F_{P}(y).
\]

(2) Since $\chi$ is diagonalized by $\left\{ s_{u,k}\coloneqq\mathsf{x}^{ku}s^{k}_{D}\mid u\in P_{k}\right\} $,
we have 
\[
\mathrm{FS}_{k}(\chi)=\max_{u\in P_{k}}\left\{ k^{-1}\log\left|s_{u,k}\right|_{tr}-f(u)\right\} .
\]
By (1), we have $\log\left|s_{u,k}\right|_{tr}(\vartheta_{y})=-\vartheta_{y}(s_{u,k})=\left\langle ku,y\right\rangle -kF_{P}(y)$.
Put it into the definition (\ref{eq:def of trop poten}), then (\ref{eq:trop of FS})
follows.

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) By (\ref{eq: Rv}) and $\varphi(v)=\varphi(\mathscr{R}v)$ for
any $v\in X^{\mathrm{an}}$, we have 
\[
\left|s\right|_{\varphi}(v)=\left|s\right|_{tr}(v)e^{-k\varphi(v)}\leq\left|s\right|_{tr}(\mathscr{R}v)e^{-k\varphi(\mathscr{R}v)}=\left|s\right|_{\varphi}(\mathscr{R}v).
\]
(2) By (\ref{eq:sup skeleton}), we only need to show that $\left|t\cdot s\right|_{\varphi}(v)=\left|s\right|_{\varphi}(v)$
for any $t\in T_{\mathbb{C}}$, $s\in R_{k}$ and $v\in\mathrm{Sk}(X^{\mathrm{an}})$.
It amounts to show $v(t\cdot s)=v(s)$. Let $s=\sum_{u\in P_{k}}c_{u}s_{u,k}$,
then $t\cdot s=\sum c_{u}t^{-ku}s_{u,k}$, where $t^{-ku}\coloneqq\mathsf{x}^{-ku}(t)\in\mathbb{C}^{*}$.
Take a maximal affine open set $X_{\sigma}$ containing the center
of $v$, and represent $s_{u,k}=\mathsf{x}^{ku-km_{\sigma}}s^{k}_{\sigma}$
by the local frame $s_{\sigma}$ of $L$, then we have 
\[
v(t\cdot s)=v\left(\sum_{u\in P_{k}}c_{u}t^{-ku}\mathsf{x}^{ku-km_{\sigma}}\right)=\min_{c_{u}\neq0}v\left(\mathsf{x}^{ku-km_{\sigma}}\right)=v(s),
\]
where the second $=$ is due to $\mathscr{R}v=v$ and (\ref{eq: Rv}).

label: prop: SN is res
title: \protect\propositionname
body_md:
\label{prop: SN is res}Assume that $\varphi:X^{\mathrm{an}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$
is torus-invariant, bounded and upper semi-continuous, then we have
$\mathrm{SN}_{k}(\varphi)(s_{u,k})=-kF^{*}_{\varphi}(u)$ for all
$k\geq1$ and $u\in P_{k}$, where $F^{*}_{\varphi}$ is the Legendre
transform of the tropical potential $F_{\varphi}$ of $\varphi$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $s\in R_{k}$, the function $v\mapsto\left|s\right|_{\varphi}=e^{-v(s)-k\varphi(v)}$
is lsc on $X^{\mathrm{an}}$, and $T^{\mathrm{an}}\subset X^{\mathrm{an}}$ is dense, so we
have $\sup_{X^{\mathrm{an}}}\left|s\right|_{\varphi}=\sup_{T^{\mathrm{an}}}\left|s\right|_{\varphi}$.
By Proposition \ref{prop:SN is inv} (1), it suffices to take the
supremum over the skeleton, so $\sup_{T^{\mathrm{an}}}\left|s\right|_{\varphi}=\sup_{y\in N_{\mathbb{R}}}\left|s\right|_{\varphi}(\vartheta_{y})$.
Hence 
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{SN}_{k}(\varphi)(s_{u,k}) & =\inf_{y\in N_{\mathbb{R}}}\left\{ \vartheta_{y}(s_{u,k})+k\varphi(\vartheta_{y})\right\} =\inf_{y\in N_{\mathbb{R}}}\left\{ \vartheta_{y}\left(\mathsf{x}^{ku}\right)+\vartheta_{y}\left(s^{k}_{D}\right)+k\varphi(\vartheta_{y})\right\} \\
 & =k\inf_{y\in N_{\mathbb{R}}}\left\{ F_{\varphi}(y)-\left\langle u,y\right\rangle \right\} =-kF^{*}_{\varphi}(u),
\end{align*}
where in the second row we used $\vartheta_{y}\left(s_{D}\right)=F_{P}(y)$
(Proposition \ref{prop: trop of FS}) and (\ref{eq:def of trop poten}).

title: \protect\definitionname
body_md:
(1) Let $V$ be a $n$-dimensional real vector space. A \emph{marked
polytope} in $V$ is a pair $(Q,A)$, where $A\subset V$ is a finite
subset (mark points) and its convex hull $Q=\mathrm{conv}(A)$ is
full-dimensional. Our primary example is $(P,P_{k})$. 

(2) For $(Q,A)$, we define an inner product space 
\[
\mathbb{R}^{A}\coloneqq\left\{ f:A\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\right\} ,\ \left\langle f,g\right\rangle \coloneqq\sum_{u\in A}f(u)g(u).
\]
The convex envelope map $\vee:\mathbb{R}^{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}(Q)$
is defined as before.

title: \protect\remarkname
body_md:
Even if $A$ is not $P_{k}$, $\vee$ also relates to the NA Fubini--Study
map. Let $M$ be a lattice, and $(Q,A)$ is a marked polytope in $M_{\mathbb{R}}$.
Suppose $A=\{m_{1},\cdots,m_{s}\}\subset M$, then the Zariski closure
of the image of map 
\[
T_{\mathbb{C}}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{s-1},\ t\mapsto\left[\mathsf{x}^{m_{1}}(t):\cdots:\mathsf{x}^{m_{s}}(t)\right]
\]
is a toric variety $X_{A}$ (may not isomorphic to $X_{Q}$). Take
the Berkovich analytification of $X_{A}$, and consider the Fubini--Study
map from the space of invariant NA norms on $\mathbb{C}^{a}$ to the space
of NA metrics on $\mathcal{O}(1)|_{X_{A}}$, we will arrive at the
envelope map $\vee$.

label: def: Chow-weight
title: \protect\definitionname
head: environment

title: \protect\definitionname
body_md:
Given a $n$-dimensional marked polytope $(Q,A)$. 

(1) A \emph{subdivision} of $(Q,A)$ is a family $S=\left\{ (Q_{i},A_{i})\mid i\in I\right\} $
of $n$-dimensional marked polytopes such that
\begin{itemize}
\item $A_{i}\subset A$ and $Q=\bigcup_{i\in I}Q_{i}$.
\item $\forall i,j\in I$, $Q_{i}\cap Q_{j}$ is empty or a common face
of $Q_{i}$ and $Q_{j}$.
\item $\forall i,j\in I$, we have $A_{i}\cap Q_{i}\cap Q_{j}=A_{j}\cap Q_{i}\cap Q_{j}$. 
\end{itemize}
Since $Q_{i}=\mathrm{conv}(A_{i})$, we can simply take $S$ as the
family $\{A_{i}\mid i\in I\}$. Subdivision $T=\{A_{i}\mid i\in I\}$
is called a \emph{triangulation} of $(Q,A)$ if all $Q_{i}$ are $n$-simplex
and $A_{i}$ is the vertex set of $Q_{i}$. 

(2) We say subdivision $S$ \emph{refines} another one $S'$ (denoted
as $S\prec S'$, by no means strictly) if each $A_{i}\in S$ is contained
in some $A^{\prime}_{j}\in S'$. It defines a partial order on the
set of all subdivisions of $(Q,A)$. The unique maximum is the trivial
subdivision $\{A\}$, and the triangulations are the minimum. A subdivision
$S$ is called \emph{full} if $\bigcup_{i\in I}A_{i}=A$, which is
equivalent to that $A_{i}=Q_{i}\cap A$ for all $i$.

(3) Regular subdivisions. For any $f:A\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$, its convex envelope
$f^{\vee}$ induces a subdivision $S(f)=\{A_{i}\mid i\in I\}$, which
is defined as follows. Let $\{Q_{i}\}_{i\in I}$ be the maximal subpolytopes
on which $f^{\vee}$ is affine, and we set 
\begin{equation}
A_{i}=\left\{ u\in A\cap Q_{i}\mid f^{\vee}(u)=f(u)\right\} .\label{eq: def S(f)}
\end{equation}
Subdivisions of the form $S(f)$ are called \textit{regular}. By \cite[Prop. 2.2.4]{de_loera_triangulations_2010},
$(Q,A)$ always admits a regular triangulation. See \cite[page 219]{gelfand_discriminants_1994}
for an irregular triangulation.

label: prop: T integral formula
title: \protect\propositionname
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\textbf{(1)} Note that the integral of $\varLambda_{T}(f)$ over a
simplex $\Delta$ of $T$ is equal to $\left|\Delta\right|$ times
the average of $f$ over the vertices of $\Delta$. Then take the
sum over simplexes, the equality follows. \textbf{(2)} The first $\Leftrightarrow$
follows from (1) and (\ref{eq: interpolate and envelope}). Suppose
$T\prec S(f)$, this means that for each simplex $\Delta$ of $T$,
there is a subpolytope $(Q_{i},A_{i})$ of $S(f)$ such that $\mathrm{vert}(\Delta)\subset A_{i}$.
By definition (\ref{eq: def S(f)}) of $S(f)$, $f^{\vee}$ is affine
over $Q_{i}\supset\Delta$ and $f^{\vee}=f$ on $A_{i}$, thus $f^{\vee}=\varLambda_{T}(f)$
on $\Delta$, so on the whole $Q$. Conversely, if $f^{\vee}=\varLambda_{T}(f)$,
then $f^{\vee}$ is affine over each simplex $\Delta$ of $T$, and
$f^{\vee}=\varLambda_{T}(f)=f$ at the vertices of $\Delta$, these
imply $T\prec S(f)$. \textbf{(3)} $\le$ follows by (1) and (\ref{eq: interpolate and envelope}).
On the other hand, there exists a triangulation $T\prec S(f)$, then
(2) implies (\ref{eq: int tent T vertex}).

title: \protect\definitionname
body_md:
The secondary polytope associated to a marked polytope $(Q,A)$ is
the following convex hull in $\mathbb{R}^{A}$, 
\[
\Sigma(A)\coloneqq\mathrm{conv}\left\{ g_{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\mid T\textrm{ is triangulation of }(Q,A)\right\} .
\]
head: environment

label: thm: structure of Sigma A
title: \protect\theoremname
body_md:
\label{thm: structure of Sigma A} Given a $n$-dimensional marked
polytope $(Q,A)$. 

(1) The affine subspace spanned by $\Sigma(A)$ is 
\begin{equation}
\left\{ g\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\Bigm|\sum_{u\in A}g(u)=1,\ \sum_{u\in A}g(u)\cdot\vec{u}=\fint_{Q}\vec{x}\ \mathrm{d}x\right\} .\label{eq:position of Sigma_A}
\end{equation}
So $\dim\Sigma(A)=\left|A\right|-n-1$. 

(2) (Subdivision-face correspondence) For a regular subdivision $S$,
we define 
\[
F(S)\coloneqq\mathrm{conv}\left\{ g_{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\mid\textrm{triangulation}\ T\prec S\right\} .
\]
Then the map $S\mapsto F(S)$ is an order-preserving bijection from
the poset of regular subdivisions of $(Q,A)$ to the face poset of
$\Sigma(A)$. The regular triangulations are in one-to-one correspondence
with the vertices of $\Sigma(A)$. 

(3) For any $f\in\mathbb{R}^{A}$, $\left\langle f,\cdot\right\rangle |_{\Sigma(A)}$
attains its minimum exactly on face $F\left(S(f)\right)$. For any
regular subdivision $S$, the outer-normal cone of $F(S)$ is 
\[
\left\{ f\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\mid\left\langle f,\cdot\right\rangle |_{\Sigma(A)}\textrm{ attains minimum on }F(S)\right\} =\left\{ f\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\mid S(f)\succ S\right\} .
\]

label: exa: pentagon
title: \protect\examplename
head: environment

title: \protect\definitionname
body_md:
A \textit{coefficient field} $\lambda$ on marked polytope $(Q,A)$ is
a Lebesgue-measurable section of $\wp$, which consists of $\left|A\right|$
functions $\lambda_{u}(\cdot)\coloneqq\lambda(\cdot)(u)$ on $Q$ such that
\[
\lambda_{u}(x)\ge0,\ \sum_{u\in A}\lambda_{u}(x)=1,\ \sum_{u\in A}\lambda_{u}(x)u=x
\]
for almost all $x\in Q$, see Example \ref{exa:model lambda}. The
\textit{generalized GKZ vector} attached to $\lambda$ is defined as
\[
g_{\lambda}:A\rightarrow\mathbb{R},\ g_{\lambda}(u)=\fint_{Q}\lambda_{u}(x)\mathrm{d}x.
\]
head: environment

label: prop:Minkowski sum
title: \protect\propositionname
body_md:
\label{prop:Minkowski sum}For a marked polytope $(Q,A)$, consider
a face $F(S)$ of $\Sigma(A)$ corresponding to a regular subdivision
$S=\left\{ (Q_{i},A_{i})\right\} _{i\in I}$. Then we have 
\[
F(S)=\sum_{i\in I}\frac{\left|Q_{i}\right|}{\left|Q\right|}\Sigma(A_{i}),
\]
where the vectors in $\Sigma(A_{i})$ are regarded as vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{A}$
by zero extension.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We say a coefficient field $\lambda$ is \textit{confined} by $S$ if
for any $i\in I$, 
\[
\lambda_{u}(\cdot)=0\text{ a.e. on }Q_{i}\text{ for }u\notin A_{i}.
\]
It suffices to show 
\[
F(S)=\left\{ g_{\lambda}\mid\lambda\text{ is confined by }S\right\} .
\]
Since if $\lambda$ is confined by $S$, after a modification on null
set, it induces a field $\lambda^{(i)}$ on $(Q_{i},A_{i})$. For any
$u\in A$, 
\[
\left|Q\right|g_{\lambda}(u)=\int_{Q}\lambda_{u}(x)=\sum_{i\in I}\int_{Q_{i}}\lambda^{(i)}_{u}(x)=\sum_{i\in I}\left|Q_{i}\right|g_{\lambda^{(i)}}(u).
\]
By (\ref{eq: SP=00003DgGKZ}), $g_{\lambda}$ belongs to the Minkowski
sum. The converse direction is similar. 

Take $f\in\mathbb{R}^{A}$ such that $S=S(f)$. If $\lambda$ is confined by
$S$, since $f^{\vee}$ is affine on $Q_{i}$ and $f^{\vee}=f$ on
$A_{i}$, so 
\[
f^{\vee}(x)=\sum_{u\in A}\lambda_{u}(x)f(u),\text{ for almost all }x\in Q.
\]
Integrating both sides, we obtain $\fint_{Q}f^{\vee}=\left\langle g_{\lambda},f\right\rangle $.
Hence $\left\langle \cdot,f\right\rangle |_{\Sigma(A)}$ attains the
minimum at $g_{\lambda}$. By Theorem \ref{thm: structure of Sigma A}
(3), we know $g_{\lambda}\in F(S(f))$. 

Conversely, given $g_{\lambda}\in F(S)$, by Jensen inequality, we have
\[
f^{\vee}(x)\le\sum_{u\in A}\lambda_{u}(x)f^{\vee}(u)\le\sum_{u\in A}\lambda_{u}(x)f(u),\ \forall x\in Q.
\]
Since $\fint_{Q}f^{\vee}=\left\langle g_{\lambda},f\right\rangle $,
two $\le$ take equality for $x\in Q\backslash E$, where $E$ is
a null set. Fix $x\in Q^{\circ}_{i}\backslash E$, the equality condition
implies that $f^{\vee}$ is affine over the set 
\[
\mathrm{cvsupp}\lambda(x)\coloneqq\mathrm{conv}\left\{ u\in A\mid\lambda_{u}(x)>0\right\} 
\]
and $f^{\vee}(u)<f(u)$ only when $\lambda_{u}(x)=0$. Since $x\in\mathrm{cvsupp}\lambda(x)$,
we have $\mathrm{cvsupp}\lambda(x)\subset Q_{i}$. By definition of $S(f)$,
these imply $\lambda_{u}(x)=0$ for all $u\notin A_{i}$, thus $\lambda$
is confined by $S$.

label: def: relative Chow-stab
title: \protect\definitionname
body_md:
\label{def: relative Chow-stab}Given a $n$-dimensional marked polytope
$(Q,A)$. 

(1) Let $\mathcal{A}$ be the space of affine functions. Since the
restriction map $\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{A}$ is injective, we
can identify $\mathcal{A}$ with the image. Let $R(A)\coloneqq\mathcal{A}^{\perp}$
be the orthogonal complement in $\mathbb{R}^{A}$, that is 
\[
R(A)=\left\{ f:A\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\Bigm|\sum_{u\in A}f(u)=0,\ \sum_{u\in A}f(u)\,\overrightarrow{u}=0\right\} .
\]
It records the affine relations between the points in $A$. Let $\Pi:\mathbb{R}^{A}\rightarrow R(A)$
be the orthogonal projection. By (\ref{eq:position of Sigma_A}),
the projection image of $\Sigma(A)$ to $\mathcal{A}$ is a single
point, denoted by $\ell_{A}$, which is the unique affine function
satisfying 
\[
\fint_{Q}\alpha=\sum_{u\in A}\alpha(u)\ell_{A}(u),\ \forall\text{ affine }\alpha.
\]

\begin{figure}
\centering
\includegraphics[viewport=0bp 0bp 1150bp 670bp,clip,scale=0.3]{position_of_SP}\caption{\label{fig: Location of second poly}Position of $\Sigma(A)$.}
\end{figure}

(2) We define the \emph{relative} Chow-weight functional $M^{\mathrm{rel}}_{A}:\mathbb{R}^{A}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$
is 
\begin{equation}
M^{\mathrm{rel}}_{A}(f)\coloneqq-\fint_{Q}\left(\Pi f\right)^{\vee}=-\fint_{Q}f^{\vee}+\left\langle f,\ell_{A}\right\rangle .
\end{equation}
It vanishes on affine functions. We say $(Q,A)$ is \emph{relatively
Chow-semistable} if $M^{\mathrm{rel}}_{A}(f)\geq0$ for all $f\in\mathbb{R}^{A}$.
Otherwise, we call $(Q,A)$ is \emph{relatively Chow-unstable}.
head: environment

title: \protect\remarkname
body_md:
When $(Q,A)=(P,P_{k})$ and $f$ takes rational numbers, $M^{\mathrm{rel}}_{A}(f)$
is the genuinely relative Chow-weight for toric variety $X_{P}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{P}R^{*}_{k}$
relative to the automorphism group $T_{\mathbb{C}}$, in the sense of \cite{szekelyhidi_extremal_2006}.
Note that our ``relative Chow-semistability'' differs from that
in \cite[Definition 5.3]{ono_algebro-geometric_2013}, which involves
the extremal affine function.
head: environment

label: thm: when semistable
title: \protect\theoremname
body_md:
\label{thm: when semistable}(1) Marked polytope $(Q,A)$ is Chow-semistable
(Definition \ref{def: Chow-weight}) if and only if the constant function
$\left|A\right|^{-1}\in\Sigma(A)$, equivalently $\ell_{A}\equiv\left|A\right|^{-1}$.

label: lem: min-max
title: \protect\lemmaname
body_md:
\label{lem: min-max}Let $K$ be a compact convex subset in an inner-product
space $W$. Suppose $0\notin K$, let $x^{*}\in K$ be the unique
point on $K$ with minimal norm. 

(1) $\left\langle x^{*},x\right\rangle \geq\left\langle x^{*},x^{*}\right\rangle $
for all $x\in K$. Moreover, $x^{*}$ is the unique point on $K$
satisfying this property. 

(2) Let $H(x)=\min_{y\in K}\left\langle x,y\right\rangle $, then
we have 
\begin{equation}
\max_{x\in W\backslash\{0\}}\frac{H(x)}{\left\Vert x\right\Vert }=\min_{y\in K}\left\Vert y\right\Vert =\left\Vert x^{*}\right\Vert .\label{eq: min-max}
\end{equation}
The maximizers for the left-hand side are $\left\{ ax^{*}\mid a>0\right\} $.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) For any $x\in K$, let $x_{t}\coloneqq tx+(1-t)x^{*}\in K$ for
$t\in[0,1]$. Since $x^{*}$ has minimal norm, we have
\[
0\leq\frac{d}{dt}\left\Vert x_{t}\right\Vert ^{2}|_{t=0}=2\left\langle x-x^{*},x^{*}\right\rangle .
\]
Conversely, if $y\in K$ satisfies this condition. It implies $\left\Vert y\right\Vert ^{2}\leq\left\langle y,x^{*}\right\rangle \leq\left\Vert y\right\Vert \left\Vert x^{*}\right\Vert $,
so $\left\Vert y\right\Vert \leq\left\Vert x^{*}\right\Vert $. Since
the minimal-norm point is unique, we have $y=x^{*}$. 

(2) For any $x\in W\backslash\{0\}$ and $y\in K$, Cauchy--Schwarz
inequality $\left\langle x,y\right\rangle \le\left\Vert x\right\Vert \left\Vert y\right\Vert $
implies 
\[
\frac{\left\langle x,y\right\rangle }{\left\Vert x\right\Vert }\le\left\Vert y\right\Vert .
\]
Take $\inf_{y\in K}$ on both sides, we obtain $\frac{H(x)}{\left\Vert x\right\Vert }\le\min_{y\in K}\left\Vert y\right\Vert =\left\Vert x^{*}\right\Vert $.
Hence $\le$ side of (\ref{eq: min-max}) follows. On the other hand,
by (1), we have 
\[
\frac{H(x^{*})}{\left\Vert x^{*}\right\Vert }=\frac{\min_{y\in K}\left\langle x^{*},y\right\rangle }{\left\Vert x^{*}\right\Vert }=\frac{\left\langle x^{*},x^{*}\right\rangle }{\left\Vert x^{*}\right\Vert }=\left\Vert x^{*}\right\Vert .
\]
Hence (\ref{eq: min-max}) holds and $x^{*}$ is a maximizer of $\bar{H}(x)\coloneqq H(x)/\left\Vert x\right\Vert $. 

Uniqueness. Suppose $x_{0},x_{1}$ are both maximizers for $\bar{H}$.
Scaling them such that $\left\Vert x_{0}\right\Vert =\left\Vert x_{1}\right\Vert =1$,
then $H(x_{0})=H(x_{1})=\max\bar{H}>0$. Consider $x_{m}=(x_{0}+x_{1})/2\neq0$.
If $x_{0}\neq x_{1}$, then we have $\left\Vert x_{m}\right\Vert <1$.
Since $H$ is concave, 
\[
H(x_{m})\ge\frac{1}{2}\left(H(x_{0})+H(x_{1})\right)=\max\bar{H}.
\]
This follows that 
\[
\bar{H}(x_{m})=\frac{H(x_{m})}{\left\Vert x_{m}\right\Vert }\ge\frac{\max\bar{H}}{\left\Vert x_{m}\right\Vert }>\max\bar{H}.
\]
That is absurd, so $x_{0}=x_{1}$.

label: thm: convex of mGKZ
title: \protect\theoremname
body_md:
\label{thm: convex of mGKZ} Let $\sigma_{A}:A\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ be the shortest
GKZ vector associated to marked polytope $(Q,A)$, then $\sigma^{\vee}_{A}|_{A}=\sigma_{A}$,
which means that $\sigma_{A}$ is convex.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider functional: 
\[
H(f)\coloneqq\fint_{Q}f^{\vee}=\min_{g\in\Sigma(A)}\left\langle f,g\right\rangle ,\ f:A\rightarrow\mathbb{R}.
\]
By Lemma \ref{lem: min-max}, maximizers of $\bar{H}(f)\coloneqq H(f)/\left\Vert f\right\Vert $
are $a\sigma_{A},\ \forall a>0$. 

Let $\rho\coloneqq\sigma^{\vee}_{A}|_{A}$, we have $0\le\rho\le\sigma_{A}$,
thus $\left\Vert \rho\right\Vert \le\left\Vert \sigma_{A}\right\Vert $.
By Proposition \ref{prop:FS vs SN} (2), we have $\rho^{\vee}=\sigma^{\vee}_{A}$.
These imply 
\[
\frac{H(\rho)}{\left\Vert \rho\right\Vert }=\frac{H(\sigma_{A})}{\left\Vert \rho\right\Vert }\ge\frac{H(\sigma_{A})}{\left\Vert \sigma_{A}\right\Vert }.
\]
Hence $\rho$ is also a maximizer of $\bar{H}$. We have $\rho=a\sigma_{A}$
for some $a>0$. But $\rho^{\vee}=\sigma^{\vee}_{A}$ implies $a=1$,
so $\rho=\sigma_{A}$.

label: thm: positive of mGKZ
title: \protect\theoremname
body_md:
\label{thm: positive of mGKZ}Let $(Q,A)$ be a marked polytope. 

(1) Let $S_{A}$ be the unique regular subdivision such that \textup{$F(S_{A})$}
is the minimal face of $\Sigma(A)$ containing $\sigma_{A}$, then
we have $S(\sigma_{A})\succ S_{A}$. We cannot exclude the possibility
that $S(\sigma_{A})\neq S_{A}$. Conversely, if $g\in\Sigma(A)$ satisfies
$g\in F\left(S(g)\right)$, then $g=\sigma_{A}$. 

(2) We have $\sigma_{A}>0$ at every point in $A$. Subdivision $S_{A}$
must be full, so is $S(\sigma_{A})$, which implies $\sigma^{\vee}_{A}|_{A}=\sigma_{A}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) By Lemma \ref{lem: min-max} (1), function $\left\langle \sigma_{A},\cdot\right\rangle |_{\Sigma(A)}$
attains its minimum at $\sigma_{A}$, so on the whole face $F(S_{A})$,
since $\sigma_{A}$ is contained in the relative interior of $F(S_{A})$.
On the other hand, Theorem \ref{thm: structure of Sigma A} (3) says
that the minimizer set is face $F\left(S(\sigma_{A})\right)$. Hence
$F\left(S(\sigma_{A})\right)\supset F(S_{A})$, so $S(\sigma_{A})\succ S_{A}$.
For the last statement, $g\in F\left(S(g)\right)$ implies that $\left\langle g,\cdot\right\rangle |_{\Sigma(A)}$
attains its minimum at $g$, by Lemma \ref{lem: min-max} (1), we
can conclude $g=\sigma_{A}$. 

(2) First we handle a simple case, namely $\sigma_{A}$ is a vertex
of $\Sigma(A)$, then $\sigma_{A}=g_{T}$ for a regular triangulation
$T$ and $S_{A}=T$. By (1), we have $S(\sigma_{A})\succ T$. Use
Proposition \ref{prop: T integral formula} (2), we have 
\[
\sigma^{\vee}_{A}=\varLambda_{T}(\sigma_{A})=\varLambda_{T}(g_{T}).
\]
By definition of GKZ vector, $g_{T}>0$ at every vertex of $T$, thus
$\varLambda_{T}(g_{T})>0$ on $Q$, i.e. $\sigma^{\vee}_{A}>0$. Since
$\sigma_{A}\ge\sigma^{\vee}_{A}|_{A}$, it implies $\sigma_{A}>0$
at every point. 

General case. Since $\sigma_{A}\in F(S_{A})$, there exists triangulations
$T_{i}\prec S_{A}$ ($1\le i\le p$) such that 
\[
\sigma_{A}=\sum^{p}_{i=1}\lambda_{i}g_{T_{i}},\ \sum^{p}_{i=1}\lambda_{i}=1,\ \lambda_{i}>0.
\]
Since $S(\sigma_{A})\succ S_{A}\succ T_{j}$, by Proposition \ref{prop: T integral formula}
(2), we have 
\[
\sigma^{\vee}_{A}=\varLambda_{T_{j}}(\sigma_{A}),\ \forall1\leq j\leq p.
\]
Since operator $\varLambda_{T_{j}}$ is linear, for each $j$ we have
\[
\varLambda_{T_{j}}(\sigma_{A})=\sum^{p}_{i=1}\lambda_{i}\varLambda_{T_{j}}(g_{T_{i}})\ge\lambda_{j}\varLambda_{T_{j}}(g_{T_{j}}),
\]
where we used $\varLambda_{T_{j}}(g_{T_{i}})\ge0$. Since $\varLambda_{T_{j}}(g_{T_{j}})>0$
on $Q$, so $\sigma^{\vee}_{A}=\varLambda_{T_{j}}(\sigma_{A})>0$.
Since $\sigma_{A}\ge\sigma^{\vee}_{A}|_{A}$, we obtain $\sigma_{A}>0$
at every point. 

Next we show $S_{A}$ is full. For any $a\in A$, we have $0<\sigma_{A}(a)=\sum^{p}_{i=1}\lambda_{i}g_{T_{i}}(a)$,
so there exists $j$ such that $g_{T_{j}}(a)>0$. By definition of
GKZ vector, it means that $a$ is a vertex of $T_{j}$. Since $T_{j}\prec S_{A}$,
$a$ is also a mark point of $S_{A}$, thus $S_{A}$ is full. Then
$S(\sigma_{A})$ is also full since $S(\sigma_{A})\succ S_{A}$.

label: thm: Gabor paper
title: \protect\theoremname
body_md:
\label{thm: Gabor paper} Given a lattice polytope $P\subset M_{\mathbb{R}}$. 

(1) Suppose $P$ is K-unstable, then 
\[
\inf\left\{ \bar{\mathbb{M}}_{P}(\eta)\mid0\neq\eta\in\mathcal{C}_{1}(P)\cap L^{2}(P)\right\} =-\left\Vert \Theta_{P}-\bar{S}\right\Vert _{L^2}
\]
admits a unique (up to scaling) minimizer $\bar{S}-\Theta_{P}\in\mathcal{C}_{1}(P)\cap L^{2}(P)$.
We call concave function $\Theta_{P}$ the optimal test-function for
$P$ (denoted by $B$ in \cite{szekelyhidi_optimal_2008}), which
satisfies variational inequality: 
\begin{equation}
\int_{\partial P}\eta\ge\int_{P}\eta\Theta_{P},\ \forall\eta\in\mathcal{C}_{1}(P)\cap L^{2}(P)\ \textrm{and}\ \int_{\partial P}\Theta_{P}=\int_{P}\Theta^{2}_{P}.\label{eq: property of Theta}
\end{equation}
When $P$ is K-semistable, we define $\Theta_{P}=\bar{S}$, above
conditions still hold. 

When $P$ is relatively K-semistable, we have $\Theta_{P}=\ell_{P}$.
If $P$ is relatively K-unstable, $\ell_{P}-\Theta_{P}$ is the unique
minimizer of $\mathbb{M}^{\mathrm{rel}}_{P}(\eta)/\left\Vert \eta\right\Vert $. 

(2) Consider the space of ``scalar curvatures'' 
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{S}(P)=\left\{ \theta\in L^{2}(P)\ \Big|\int_{\partial P}\eta\ge\int_{P}\eta\theta,\ \forall\eta\in\mathcal{C}_{1}(P)\cap L^{2}(P)\right\} ,
\end{equation}
then $\Theta_{P}$ is the unique element in $\mathcal{S}(P)$ with
minimal $L^{2}$-norm. Recall that if $u:P\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is the symplectic
potential of an invariant Kähler metric, its scalar curvature is $S(u)=-\sum_{i,j}\partial_{i}\partial_{j}u^{ij}\in\mathcal{S}(P)$.

(3) Consider the Calabi flow on $X_{P}$ with invariant initial data,
which can be reduced into evolution equation on $P$: 
\[
\dot{u}_{t}=-S(u_{t})=\sum_{i,j}\partial_{i}\partial_{j}u^{ij}_{t}.
\]
Assume it admits long-time solutions, then $S(u_{t})\stackrel{L^{2}}{\rightarrow}\Theta_{P}$
as $t\rightarrow\infty$. 

(4) (canonical semi-stable decomposition) Assume $P$ is relatively
K-unstable and $\Theta_{P}$ is piecewise affine. Let $Q\subset P$
be a maximal subpolytope over which $\Theta_{P}$ is affine, then
$Q$ is relatively K-semistable in the following sense: 
\begin{equation}
\int_{\partial Q\cap\partial P}\eta\ \mathrm{d}\sigma\ge\int_{Q}\eta\Theta_{P}\ \mathrm{d}x,\ \forall\eta\in\mathcal{C}(Q).\label{eq: semi-decom}
\end{equation}
head: environment

title: \protect\remarkname
body_md:
Under the assumptions in (4), we can deduce that each subpolytope
$Q$ must have a facet which is entirely contained in $\partial P$.
If not, we have $\left|\partial Q\cap\partial P\right|_{\mathrm{d}\sigma}=0$.
Take $\eta$ in (\ref{eq: semi-decom}) to be the affine functions
extending $\pm\Theta|_{Q}$, it implies 
\[
\int_{Q}\Theta^{2}=\int_{\partial Q\cap\partial P}\Theta\ \mathrm{d}\sigma=0.
\]
So $\Theta\equiv0$ on $Q$. Since $\Theta$ is concave, this implies
$\Theta\leq0$ on $P$, but this contradicts with $\int_{P}\Theta=V_{\partial P,\mathrm{d}\sigma}>0$,
which follows from (\ref{eq: property of Theta}).

title: Proof
body_md:
For any $\eta\in\mathcal{C}_{1}(P)\cap L^{2}(P)$, (\ref{eq: property of Theta})
implies 
\[
\int_{\partial P}\eta\geq\int_{P}\eta\Theta\geq-\left\Vert \eta\right\Vert _{L^2}\left\Vert \Theta\right\Vert _{L^2}\geq-\frac{1}{2}\left\Vert \eta\right\Vert ^{2}_{L^2}-\frac{1}{2}\left\Vert \Theta\right\Vert ^{2}_{L^2}.
\]
Thus $\Psi(\eta)\geq-\frac{1}{2}\left\Vert \Theta\right\Vert ^{2}_{L^2}$.
This lower bound is achieved by $\eta=-\Theta$ since $\int_{P}\Theta^{2}=\int_{\partial P}\Theta$.
The uniqueness follows from the strict convexity of $L^{2}$-norm.

title: \protect\remarkname
body_md:
\begin{enumerate}
\item
Since $-\Theta_{P}$ is a minimizer, for any convex $\eta$, we have
$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\Psi(t\eta-\Theta_{P})|_{t=0}\ge0$
and $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\Psi(-t\Theta_{P})|_{t=1}=0$.
These give us (\ref{eq: property of Theta}). Conversely, (\ref{eq: property of Theta})
can imply that $-\Theta_{P}$ is the minimizer of $\Psi$, since for any
convex $\eta$, we have 
\[
\Psi\left(\eta\right)-\Psi\left(-\Theta\right)=\frac{1}{2}\int_{P}\left(\eta+\Theta\right)^{2}+\int_{\partial P}\eta-\int_{P}\eta\Theta\ge0.
\]

\item 
The functional below is more closely related to $\mathbb{M}_{P}$
than $\Psi$, 
\begin{equation}
\breve{\mathbb{M}}_{P}(\eta)\coloneqq\mathbb{M}_{P}(\eta)+\frac{1}{2}\left\Vert \eta\right\Vert ^{2}_{L^{2}}=\Psi(\eta-\bar{S})+\frac{1}{2}\bar{S}^{2}V_{P}.\label{eq: horn M}
\end{equation}
Its relative version is 
\[
\breve{\mathbb{M}}^{\mathrm{rel}}_{P}(\eta)\coloneqq\mathbb{M}^{\mathrm{rel}}_{P}(\eta)+\frac{1}{2}\left\Vert \eta\right\Vert ^{2}_{L^{2}}=\Psi(\eta-\ell_{P})+\frac{1}{2}\int_{P}\ell^{2}_{P}.
\]
Apparently, minimizing these functionals is equivalent to minimizing
$\Psi$. 
\end{enumerate}

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $u=-\Theta$, we show $\inf_{P}u=\inf_{\partial P}u$. If this
is not true, let $m\coloneqq\inf_{P}u<\inf_{\partial P}u$. Since
$\int_{P}\Theta=\left|\partial P\right|_{\mathrm{d}\sigma}>0$, we
know $m<0$. Take $\delta>0$ such that $0>m+\delta<\inf_{\partial P}u$.
Consider $u'=\max\left\{ u,m+\delta\right\} $. Since $u\geq\inf_{\partial P}u>m+\delta$
on $\partial P$, we have $u'=u$ on $\partial P$. Then it is easy
to see
\[
\Psi(u')=\frac{1}{2}\int_{P}u'^{2}+\int_{\partial P}u'<\frac{1}{2}\int_{P}u^{2}+\int_{\partial P}u=\Psi(u).
\]
It is absurd since $u$ is a minimizer of $\Psi$.

title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof of Li-Lian-Sheng}For readers to make comparisons, we
use the same notations as \cite[Theorem 6.2]{li_extremal_2023}. For
example, coordinates on $N_{\mathbb{R}}$ are denoted by $x$, and $\xi$
for $M_{\mathbb{R}}$. 

Translate $P$ such that $0\in\mathrm{int}P$, then $a_{\rho}>0$.
Let 
\[
u\coloneqq-\Theta_{P}:P\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\},
\]
which is lsc, convex and taking finite values on $P^{*}$. We set
$u=+\infty$ outside $P$. Fix any $p^{o}\in\partial u(0)$, let $\ell(\xi)\coloneqq u(0)+\left\langle p^{o},\xi\right\rangle $
be the attached support function. Define $u^{o}\coloneqq u-\ell$,
we have $u^{o}(\xi)\geq u^{o}(0)=0$ for $\forall\xi\in P$. Let 
\[
f^{o}(x)\coloneqq\left(u^{o}\right)^{*}(x)\coloneqq\sup_{\xi\in P}\left\langle x,\xi\right\rangle -u^{o}(\xi),\ x\in N_{\mathbb{R}}
\]
be the Legendre dual of $u^{o}$. We also have $f^{o}(x)\geq f^{o}(0)=0$.
Since $0\in\mathrm{int}P$, there exists a closed ball $B\subset\mathrm{int}P$
centered at $0$, then we have 
\[
I_{P}\leq u^{o}\leq I_{B}+\sup_{B}u^{o},
\]
where $I_{B}$ is the convex characteristic function of $B$, i.e.
$I_{B}=0$ on $B$ and $=+\infty$ otherwise. Taking the Legendre
dual, we obtain 
\[
\sup_{\xi\in P}\left\langle x,\xi\right\rangle \geq f^{o}(x)\geq\sup_{\xi\in B}\left\langle x,\xi\right\rangle -\sup_{B}u^{o},\ x\in N_{\mathbb{R}}.
\]
It implies that the sublevel set 
\[
S_{f^{o}}(h)\coloneqq\left\{ x\in N_{\mathbb{R}}\mid f^{o}(x)\leq h\right\} 
\]
is compact and convex. 

We introduce the key construction in \cite[before Lem. 3.9]{li_extremal_2023}.
For $h>0$, we define the \textit{Legendre truncation} of $u^{o}$
is 
\[
u^{o}_{h}(\xi)\coloneqq\sup_{x:f^{o}(x)\leq h}\left\langle x,\xi\right\rangle -f^{o}(x)=\left(\left(u^{o}\right)^{*}+I_{S_{f^{o}}(h)}\right)^{*}(\xi).
\]
It is the tropical analogue of the Fourier truncation. Intuitionally,
for $h\gg1$, $u^{o}_{h}$ is the flattening of $u$ over the region
with large slope. Since $f^{o}\geq0$, it is easy to see 
\begin{equation}
\sup_{f^{o}(x)\leq h}\left\langle x,\xi\right\rangle -h\leq u^{o}_{h}\leq u^{o},\ \sup_{f^{o}(x)\leq h}\left\langle x,\xi\right\rangle .\label{eq:bound of uo_h}
\end{equation}
Set 
\[
u_{h}\coloneqq u^{o}_{h}+\ell\leq u^{o}+\ell=u,
\]
which is nondecreasing in $h$. We will show that 
\[
u_{h}=u,\ \text{on }P\text{ when }h\gg1.
\]
The proof proceeds in several steps. For $h>0$, let 
\[
W_{h}\coloneqq\partial f^{o}\left\{ f^{o}\leq h\right\} \subset P,
\]
which is compact by \cite[Lemma A.22]{figalli_monge-ampere_2017},
and may not be convex.

\textbf{(a)} We show $u^{o}_{h}=u^{o}$ on $W_{h}$. Suppose $\xi\in\partial f^{o}(x)$
with $f^{o}(x)\leq h$, then we have 
\[
u^{o}_{h}(\xi)\geq\left\langle x,\xi\right\rangle -f^{o}(x)=u^{o}(\xi),
\]
where the equality is due to $\xi\in\partial f^{o}(x)$. Since $u^{o}_{h}\leq u^{o}$,
it forces $u^{o}_{h}(\xi)=u^{o}(\xi)$.

\textbf{(b)} We show that $W_{h}$ is a star set, i.e. if $\xi\in W_{h}$
then $t\xi\in W_{h}$ for any $t\in[0,1)$.

Suppose $\xi\in\partial f^{o}(x)$ with $f^{o}(x)\leq h$. Take any
$x_{t}\in\partial u^{o}(t\xi)$, since $t\xi\in\partial f^{o}(x_{t})$,
it suffices to show $f^{o}(x_{t})\leq h$. Since $x\in\partial u^{o}(\xi)$
and $x_{t}\in\partial u^{o}(t\xi)$, by the definition of subdifferentials,
we have 
\begin{align*}
u^{o}(t\xi) & \geq u^{o}(\xi)+\left\langle x,t\xi-\xi\right\rangle ,\\
u^{o}(\xi) & \geq u^{o}(t\xi)+\left\langle x_{t},\xi-t\xi\right\rangle .
\end{align*}
They imply $\left\langle x_{t},\xi\right\rangle \leq\left\langle x,\xi\right\rangle $.
Then we have 
\begin{align*}
f^{o}(x_{t}) & =\left\langle x_{t},t\xi\right\rangle -u^{o}(t\xi)\leq t\left\langle x,\xi\right\rangle -u^{o}(t\xi)\\
 & \leq t\left\langle x,\xi\right\rangle -\left[u^{o}(\xi)+\left\langle x,t\xi-\xi\right\rangle \right]\\
 & =\left\langle x,\xi\right\rangle -u^{o}(\xi)=f^{o}(x)\leq h.
\end{align*}
Since $W_{h}$ is a star set, we can describe it as 
\[
W_{h}=\left\{ tq\mid q\in\partial P,0\leq t\leq r_{h}(q)\leq1\right\} ,
\]
where $r_{h}:\partial P\rightarrow[0,1]$ is a function. Since $W_{h}$ is
closed, $r_{h}(q)$ is usc in $q$ and nondecreasing in $h$. We simply
write $r_{q}\coloneqq r_{h}(q)$. 

\textbf{(c)} We show that $\lim_{h\rightarrow\infty}r_{h}(q)=1$ uniformly
for $q\in\partial P$. 

For any $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, let $P_{\varepsilon}\coloneqq(1-\varepsilon)P$.
By \cite[Lemma A.22]{figalli_monge-ampere_2017}, $\partial u^{o}\left(P_{\varepsilon}\right)$
is a compact set in $N_{\mathbb{R}}$. We claim that 
\[
P_{\varepsilon}\subset W_{h}\ \text{when }h>H_{\varepsilon}\coloneqq\sup_{\partial u^{o}\left(P_{\varepsilon}\right)}f^{o}.
\]
For any $\xi\in P_{\varepsilon}$, take $x\in\partial u^{o}(\xi)\subset\partial u^{o}\left(P_{\varepsilon}\right)$,
we have $\xi\in\partial f^{o}(x)$ and $f^{o}(x)\leq H_{\varepsilon}$,
so $\xi\in W_{h>H_{\varepsilon}}$. By the definition of $r_{h}(q)$,
we have 
\[
1-\varepsilon\leq r_{h}(q)\leq1,\ \forall q\in\partial P
\]
when $h>H_{\varepsilon}$. Hence \textbf{(c)} follows. 

\textbf{(d)} For any $q\in\partial P$, $u^{o}_{h}$ is affine restricting
on the ray $\left\{ tq\mid t\geq r_{q}\coloneqq r_{h}(q)\right\} $.
Explicitly, we have 
\[
u^{o}_{h}(tq)=\frac{t}{r_{q}}\left(u^{o}(r_{q}q)+h\right)-h,\ \text{for }t\geq r_{q}.
\]
Proof: For any $q\in\partial P$, fix a $t>r_{q}$. Since $S_{f^{o}}(h)$
is compact, the supremum 
\[
u^{o}_{h}(tq)\coloneqq\sup_{x\in S_{f^{o}}(h)}\left\langle x,\xi\right\rangle -f^{o}(x)=\sup_{x\in N_{\mathbb{R}}}\left\langle x,tq\right\rangle -\left(f^{o}(x)+I_{S_{f^{o}}(h)}(x)\right)
\]
is attained by some $x^{*}\in S_{f^{o}}(h)$, and this occurs if and
only if 
\begin{equation}
tq\in\partial\left(f^{o}+I_{S_{f^{o}}(h)}\right)(x^{*})=\partial f^{o}(x^{*})+\partial I_{S_{f^{o}}(h)}(x^{*}).\label{eq:Moreau-Rockafellar}
\end{equation}
The last equality is due to Moreau--Rockafellar theorem.

If $x^{*}$ does not lie on the boundary of $S_{f^{o}}(h)$, (\ref{eq:Moreau-Rockafellar})
implies $tq\in\partial f^{o}(x^{*})\subset W_{h}$. That is absurd
since $t>r_{q}$. Hence $x^{*}$ must lie on the boundary and $f^{o}(x^{*})=h$.

By the definition of subdifferentials, we note that 
\begin{align*}
\partial I_{S_{f^{o}}(h)}(x^{*}) & =\left\{ \xi\mid\left\langle x-x^{*},\xi\right\rangle \leq0,\ \forall x\in S_{f^{o}}(h)\right\} \\
 & =\left\{ \lambda\eta\mid\lambda\geq0,\ \eta\in\partial f^{o}(x^{*})\right\} .
\end{align*}
Thus by (\ref{eq:Moreau-Rockafellar}), we can write $tq=\eta_{1}+\lambda\eta_{2}$
with $\eta_{i}\in\partial f^{o}(x^{*})$ and $\lambda>0$. 

For any $a\geq1$, we find 
\[
atq=\eta_{1}+\left(a-1+a\lambda\right)\frac{\left(a-1\right)\eta_{1}+a\lambda\eta_{2}}{a-1+a\lambda}\in\partial f^{o}(x^{*})+\partial I_{S_{f^{o}}(h)}(x^{*}),
\]
where the convexity of $\partial f^{o}(x^{*})$ is used. This inclusion
relation implies that the supremum 
\[
u^{o}_{h}(atq)\coloneqq\sup_{x\in N_{\mathbb{R}}}\left\langle x,atq\right\rangle -\left(f^{o}(x)+I_{S_{f^{o}}(h)}(x)\right)
\]
is still attained by $x^{*}$. So $u^{o}_{h}(atq)=\left\langle x^{*},atq\right\rangle -h$
for all $a\geq1$. Since $t$ can be arbitrarily close to $r_{q}$,
\textbf{(d)} follows. 

\textbf{(e)} It is ready to show $u=u_{h}$ for $h\gg1$. Let 
\[
v_{h}\coloneqq u-u_{h}=u^{o}-u^{o}_{h}\geq0.
\]
By property \textbf{(c)}, for any $q\in\partial P$, the function
$[r_{q},1]\ni t\mapsto v_{h}(tq)$ is convex and vanishes at $t=r_{q}$
by \textbf{(a)}. It implies that this function is nondecreasing, so
\begin{equation}
v_{h}(tq)\leq v_{h}(q),\ \forall t\in[r_{q},1].\label{eq:controll v_h}
\end{equation}
Note that $v_{h}(q)<\infty$, when $q$ lies in the relative interior
of facets, since $u<+\infty$ on $P^{*}$. 

To estimate the integrals over $P$, we decompose $P=\bigcup_{\rho\in\mathcal{F}_{P}(1)}P_{\rho}$,
where $P_{\rho}$ is the cone with apex $0$ and base $F_{\rho}$
(facet of $P$ associated to $\rho$). Consider the map 
\[
[0,1]\times F_{\rho}\rightarrow P_{\rho},\ \left(t,q\right)\mapsto tq.
\]
One can check that the pullback of Lebesgue measure $\mathrm{d}\mu$
along this map is $a_{\rho}t^{n-1}\mathrm{d}t\wedge\mathrm{d\sigma}$. 

By \textbf{(a)}, $v_{h}(tq)=0$ when $t\in[0,r_{q}]$. Use (\ref{eq:controll v_h}),
we have 
\[
\int_{P_{\rho}}v_{h}\mathrm{d}\mu=a_{\rho}\int_{F_{\rho}}\int^{1}_{r_{q}}v_{h}(tq)t^{n-1}\mathrm{d}t\mathrm{d\sigma}\leq\frac{a_{\rho}}{n}\int_{F_{\rho}}\left(1-r^{n}_{q}\right)v_{h}(q)\mathrm{d\sigma}.
\]
Take the sum over $\rho$, we obtain 
\begin{equation}
0\leq\int_{P}v_{h}\mathrm{d}\mu\leq\frac{\max_{\rho}a_{\rho}}{n}\left(1-\inf_{q\in\partial P}r^{n}_{q}\right)\int_{\partial P}v_{h}\mathrm{d\sigma}.\label{eq:controll vh int}
\end{equation}
Compare the $L^{2}$-norms, 
\begin{align*}
\int_{P}u^{2}_{h}-\int_{P}u^{2} & =\int_{P}\left(u^{o}_{h}+\ell\right)^{2}-\int_{P}\left(u^{o}+\ell\right)^{2}=\int_{P}\left(u^{o}_{h}\right)^{2}-\int_{P}\left(u^{o}\right)^{2}-2\int_{P}v_{h}\ell\\
 & \leq2\max_{P}\left|\ell\right|\int_{P}v_{h}\leq\frac{2}{n}\max_{P}\left|\ell\right|\max_{\rho}a_{\rho}\left(1-\inf_{q\in\partial P}r^{n}_{q}\right)\int_{\partial P}v_{h}\mathrm{d\sigma}.
\end{align*}
where $\int_{P}\left(u^{o}_{h}\right)^{2}\leq\int_{P}\left(u^{o}\right)^{2}$
is due to $0\leq u^{o}_{h}\leq u^{o}$. 

We obtain a comparison of functional values, 
\[
\left(\frac{1}{2}\int_{P}u^{2}_{h}+\int_{\partial P}u_{h}\right)-\left(\frac{1}{2}\int_{P}u^{2}+\int_{\partial P}u\right)\leq\left[C\left(1-\inf_{q\in\partial P}r^{n}_{q}\right)-1\right]\int_{\partial P}v_{h}\mathrm{d\sigma}.
\]
By \textbf{(c)}, we know $\inf_{q\in\partial P}r^{n}_{q}\rightarrow1$. So
there exists $h_{0}>0$, when $h>h_{0}$, the RHS $\leq-\frac{1}{2}\int_{\partial P}v_{h}$.
Since $u$ is a minimizer of (\ref{eq: Inoue functional}), we must
have $\int_{\partial P}v_{h}\mathrm{d\sigma}=0$ for $h>h_{0}$. By
(\ref{eq:controll vh int}), it implies $\int_{P}v_{h}=0$, so $u=u_{h}$
almost everywhere. Since $u$ is continuous on $P^{*}$ and $u_{h}$
is continuous everywhere, so $u=u_{h}$ on $P^{*}$. Note $u$ is
also lsc, so 
\[
u_{h}=u,\ \text{on }P\text{ when }h>h_{0}.
\]
Moreover, by (\ref{eq:bound of uo_h}), we have 
\[
\partial u\left(\mathrm{int}P\right)=\partial u_{h}\left(\mathrm{int}P\right)\subset\partial u_{h}\left(M_{\mathbb{R}}\right)=S_{f^{o}}(h)+p^{o}
\]
when $h>h_{0}$. Since $S_{f^{o}}(h)$ is bounded, so is $\partial u\left(\mathrm{int}P\right)$.

label: thm: min Psi_k
title: \protect\theoremname
head: environment

label: eq: min Psi_k
title: Proof
body_md:
\textbf{Step 1}. Reduce the minimization problem 
\begin{equation}
\inf\left\{ \Psi_{k}(\eta)\mid\eta\in\mathcal{C}(P)\right\} \label{eq: min Psi_k}
\end{equation}
to (\ref{eq: minimize Mk horn}). For any $\eta\in\mathcal{C}(P)$,
let $\eta_{k}=\left(\eta|_{P_{k}}\right)^{\vee}$. By Proposition
\ref{prop:FS vs SN}, we have $\eta_{k}\ge\eta$ and $\eta_{k}|_{P_{k}}=\eta|_{P_{k}}$,
these imply $\Psi_{k}(\eta_{k})\leq\Psi_{k}(\eta)$ with equality
only if $\eta_{k}=\eta$. Hence problem (\ref{eq: min Psi_k}) can
be reduced to 
\begin{equation}
\inf\left\{ \Psi_{k}(\eta)\mid\eta\in\mathrm{PL}(P,P_{k})\right\} ,\label{eq: inf Q horn PL}
\end{equation}
recall $\mathrm{PL}(P,P_{k})$ is the image of envelope map $\vee:\mathbb{R}^{P_{k}}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}(P)$. 

By Proposition \ref{prop:FS vs SN} (3), $\vee:\mathcal{C}(P_{k})\rightarrow\mathrm{PL}(P,P_{k})$
is a bijection. Hence we can change the domain of (\ref{eq: inf Q horn PL})
to $\mathcal{C}(P_{k})$. Since for any $f\in\mathcal{C}(P_{k})$,
we have $f^{\vee}|_{P_{k}}=f$, it follows that 
\[
\Psi_{k}\left(f^{\vee}\right)=\frac{1}{2k^{n}}\sum_{u\in P_{k}}f(u)^{2}+\frac{2}{k^{n-1}}\left(\sum_{u\in P_{k}}f(u)-k^{n}\int_{P}f^{\vee}\right)\eqqcolon\breve{M}_{P_{k}}(f).
\]
By changing the domain, problem (\ref{eq: inf Q horn PL}) is equivalent
to 
\begin{equation}
\inf\left\{ \breve{M}_{P_{k}}(f)\mid f\in\mathcal{C}(P_{k})\right\} .\label{eq: minimize Mk horn}
\end{equation}

\textbf{Step 2}. We claim that 
\[
f^{*}\coloneqq2V_{P}k^{n+1}\left(\sigma_{k}-\frac{1}{V_{P}k^{n}}\right)
\]
is actually the unique minimizer of $\breve{M}_{P_{k}}$ over larger
space $\mathbb{R}^{P_{k}}$. The uniqueness is obvious, since $\breve{M}_{P_{k}}$
is strictly convex. 

Once this claim holds, since $f^{*}\in\mathcal{C}(P_{k})$ by Theorem
\ref{thm: convex of mGKZ} and Proposition \ref{prop:FS vs SN} (2),
it is also the unique minimizer of (\ref{eq: minimize Mk horn}).
Then trace back the reductions in Step 1, we see $\left(f^{*}\right)^{\vee}$
is the unique minimizer of $\Psi_{k}$, that is (\ref{eq:quan minimizer}). 

Next we verify the above claim. For any $f\in\mathbb{R}^{P_{k}}$, by (\ref{eq: Int tent formula}),
we have 
\[
\frac{1}{V_{P}}\int_{P}f^{\vee}=\min_{g\in\Sigma(P_{k})}\left\langle f,g\right\rangle \le\left\langle f,\sigma_{k}\right\rangle =\left\langle f,\sigma_{k}-\frac{1}{V_{P}k^{n}}\right\rangle +\frac{1}{V_{P}k^{n}}\sum_{u\in P_{k}}f(u),
\]
\[
\left\langle f,\sigma_{k}-\frac{1}{V_{P}k^{n}}\right\rangle \le\left\Vert f\right\Vert \left\Vert \sigma_{k}-\frac{1}{V_{P}k^{n}}\right\Vert \le\frac{1}{4V_{P}k^{n+1}}\left\Vert f\right\Vert ^{2}+V_{P}k^{n+1}\left\Vert \sigma_{k}-\frac{1}{V_{P}k^{n}}\right\Vert ^{2}.
\]
Combine these inequalities together, we obtain 
\[
\breve{M}_{P_{k}}(f)\geq-2V^{2}_{P}k^{n+2}\left\Vert \sigma_{k}-\frac{1}{V_{P}k^{n}}\right\Vert ^{2}.
\]
Next we check that this lower bound is achieved by $f^{*}$. Denote
$f^{*}=a(\sigma_{k}-c)$ for short, where $a=2V_{P}k^{n+1}$ and $c=\frac{1}{V_{P}k^{n}}$.
Using identities 
\[
\sum_{u\in P_{k}}\sigma_{k}(u)=1\text{ and }\int_{P}\sigma^{\vee}_{k}=V_{P}\left\Vert \sigma_{k}\right\Vert ^{2},
\]
we compute 
\begin{align*}
\sum_{u\in P_{k}}f^{*}(u)-k^{n}\int_{P}\left(f^{*}\right)^{\vee} & =a\left(2-c\left|P_{k}\right|-c^{-1}\left\Vert \sigma_{k}\right\Vert ^{2}\right)=-\frac{a}{c}\left\Vert \sigma_{k}-c\right\Vert ^{2}.
\end{align*}
Hence 
\[
\breve{M}_{P_{k}}(f^{*})=\frac{a^{2}}{2k^{n}}\left\Vert \sigma_{k}-c\right\Vert ^{2}-\frac{2}{k^{n-1}}\frac{a}{c}\left\Vert \sigma_{k}-c\right\Vert ^{2}=-2V^{2}_{P}k^{n+2}\left\Vert \sigma_{k}-c\right\Vert ^{2}.
\]

title: \protect\remarkname
body_md:
The toric version of general functional $\breve{\mathbb{Q}}_{k}$
in \cite{yao_maximal_2025} is  
\[
\frac{1}{2k^{n}}\sum_{u\in P_{k}}\eta(u)^{2}+2kV_{P}\left(\frac{1}{\left|P_{k}\right|}\sum_{u\in P_{k}}\eta(u)-\fint_{P}\eta\right),
\]
which pointwisely converges to $\breve{\mathbb{M}}_{P}(\eta)$ (\ref{eq: horn M}).
However, it equals to 
\[
\Psi_{k}\left(\eta-\frac{s_{k}}{r_{k}}\right)+\frac{V_{P}s^{2}_{k}}{2r_{k}},\ r_{k}=\frac{\left|P_{k}\right|}{V_{P}k^{n}}\rightarrow1,\ s_{k}=2k(r_{k}-1)\rightarrow\bar{S}.
\]
Hence for fixed $k$, minimizing the above functional amounts to minimizing
$\Psi_{k}$. Indeed, by using Remark \ref{rem-quadmin} and the proof of Theorem \ref{thm: Chow destabi}, we know that $\breve{\mathbb{Q}}_{k}$ obtains the minimum at $\eta_k=2k^{n+1}V_P(\sigma_k^\vee-\frac{1}{|P_k|})=2k^{n+1}V_P\sigma_k^\vee-\frac{2k}{r_k}$ and one sees that $\eta_k-\frac{s_k}{r_k}=\psi_k$ from \eqref{eq:quan minimizer}.

title: Proof
body_md:
First we triangulate $P$ using diagonals. For each resulting simplex
$\Delta$, take an affine bijection from the standard simplex $\Delta_{n}=\mathrm{conv}\{0,e_{1},\dots,e_{n}\}$
to $\Delta$. The Freudenthal--Kuhn triangulation of $\Delta_{n}$
uses the points in $k^{-1}\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ and consists of $k^{n}$
simplices. Via the affine map, it induces a triangulation $T$ of
$(P,P_{k})$, see Figure \ref{fig:Kuhn}. The number of simplices
adjacent to a point $u\in P_{k}$ is bounded above by a constant which
is independent of $k$. This implies $g_{T}\le C_{P}k^{-n}$ for a
constant $C_{P}$. 
\begin{figure}[H]
\begin{centering}
\includegraphics[clip,scale=0.2]{Kuhn}
\par\end{centering}
\caption{\label{fig:Kuhn}Freudenthal--Kuhn triangulation, $k=4$}
\end{figure}

Finally, by (\ref{eq: Int tent formula}), we have 
\[
\fint_{P}\phi\le\fint_{P}\left(\phi|_{P_{k}}\right)^{\vee}\le\sum_{u\in P_{k}}g_{T}(u)\phi(u)\le\frac{C_{P}}{k^{n}}\sum_{u\in P_{k}}\phi(u).
\]

label: exa:model lambda
title: \protect\examplename
body_md:
\label{exa:model lambda} Consider an $n$-dimensional lattice rectangular box $Q=\prod^{n}_{i=1}[0,m_{i}]\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$
with $m_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$. There is a canonical division of
$Q$ into $\left(\prod^{n}_{i=1}m_{i}\right)$ number of $n$-dimensional
unit lattice square boxes. For $x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\in Q$ belongs
to box $\prod^{n}_{i=1}[j_{i},j_{i}+1]$ with $j_{i}\in\{0,1,\dots,m_{i}-1\}$,
we have 
\[
x_{i}=\left(1-(x_{i}-j_{i})\right)\cdot j_{i}+(x_{i}-j_{i})(j_{i}+1)=\sum^{m_{i}}_{j=0}(1-|x_{i}-j|)_{+}\cdot j,
\]
where $t_{+}=\max\{t,0\}$. Define a coefficient field on $Q$: for
any $u\in Q\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}$, set 
\[
\lambda_{u}(x)=\prod^{n}_{i=1}(1-|x_{i}-u_{i}|)_{+}.
\]
Then for $x\in Q$, the following equalities are satisfied: 
\begin{eqnarray*}
\sum_{u\in Q\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}}\lambda_{u}(x) & = & \prod^{n}_{i=1}\sum^{m_{i}}_{u_{i}=0}(1-|x_{i}-u_{i}|)_{+}=1,\\
\sum_{u\in Q\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}}\lambda_{u}(x)u_{k} & = & \sum^{m_{k}}_{u_{k}=0}(1-|x_{k}-u_{k}|)_{+}u_{k}\cdot\prod_{i\neq k}\sum^{m_{i}}_{u_{i}=0}(1-|x_{i}-u_{i}|)_{+}\\
 & = & x_{k}.
\end{eqnarray*}
It is easy to see that for each $x\in Q$, $\lambda_{u}(x)>0$ only
when $d_{\infty}(u,x)<1$. In other words, the support of $\lambda(x)$
is contained in a single unit square. Moreover, due to the separation
of variables, we easily calculate: 
\[
\int_{Q}\lambda_{u}(x)\mathrm{d}x=2^{-\mathrm{cd}(u)},
\]
where $\mathrm{cd}(u)$ is the the number of facets of $Q$ that contain
$u$. For any $\phi\in\mathcal{C}(Q)$, (\ref{eq:lam give bound})
gives the estimate: 
\[
\int_{Q}\phi\mathrm{d}x\le\sum_{u\in Q\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}}2^{-\mathrm{cd}(u)}\phi(u).
\]

label: thm-fine
title: \protect\theoremname
head: environment
name: Fine estimate

title: Proof
body_md:
For a vertex $v$ of $P$, let $e^{1}_{v},\dots,e^{n}_{v}\in M$ be
the primitive generators of the edges emanating from $v$, which form
a lattice basis since $P$ is Delzant. Let $C_{v}$ be the vertex
cone at $v$, define a map 
\[
\Gamma_{v}:\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\ge0}\rightarrow C_{v},\ \Gamma_{v}(t)=v+\frac{t_{1}}{k}e^{1}_{v}+\cdots+\frac{t_{n}}{k}e^{n}_{v},
\]
which is bijective between $\mathbb{\mathbb{Z}}^{n}_{\ge0}$ and $C_{v}\cap k^{-1}M$.

First we define a coefficient field for $\left(\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\ge0},\mathbb{\mathbb{Z}}^{n}_{\ge0}\right)$,
then transport it to $P$ via the map $\Gamma_{v}$, and finally patch
them together. For $n=1$, let 
\[
b_{0}(t)=(1-t)_{+},\ b_{j}(t)=\left(1-\left|t-j\right|\right)_{+}\text{ for }j\ge1.
\]
Easy to check 
\[
\sum_{j\ge0}b_{j}(t)=1,\ \sum_{j\ge0}b_{j}(t)\cdot j=t,\ \forall t\ge0.
\]
We extend it to $\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\ge0}$ by taking the tensor product,
\[
B_{m}(t)\coloneqq b_{m_{1}}(t_{1})\cdots b_{m_{n}}(t_{n}),\text{ for }m\in\mathbb{\mathbb{Z}}^{n}_{\ge0}\text{ and }t\in\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\ge0}.
\]
Then we have 
\begin{equation}
\sum_{m\in\mathbb{\mathbb{Z}}^{n}_{\ge0}}B_{m}(t)=1,\ \sum_{m\in\mathbb{\mathbb{Z}}^{n}_{\ge0}}B_{m}(t)\cdot m=t,\ \forall t\in\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\ge0}.\label{eq: field B}
\end{equation}
Next we patch 
\[
\left\{ B_{\Gamma^{-1}_{v}u}(\Gamma^{-1}_{v}\cdot):P\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\mid u\in P_{k}\right\} _{v}
\]
 together via a partition of unity. Suppose 
\[
P=\left\{ x\in M_{\mathbb{R}}\mid l_{F}(x)\ge0,\text{ for all facet }F\right\} .
\]
Fix a small $\varepsilon>0$, for a vertex $v$ of $P$, set 
\[
U_{v}\coloneqq\left\{ x\in P\mid l_{F}(x)>\varepsilon,\ \forall F\not\ni v\right\} .
\]
Then $\left\{ U_{v}\right\} _{v}$ forms an open cover of $P$. Take
a partition of unity $\left\{ \rho_{v}:P\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\right\} _{v}$ which
are smooth up to $\partial P$ and satisfy 
\[
\sum_{v}\rho_{v}=1,\ \mathrm{supp}\rho_{v}\subset U_{v}.
\]
For $x\in P$, let $F_{x}$ be the smallest face containing $x$.
Note that $\rho_{v}(x)=0$ if $v$ is not a vertex of $F_{x}$.

We define 
\[
\lambda_{u}(x)=\sum_{v\in\mathrm{vert}P}\rho_{v}(x)B_{\Gamma^{-1}_{v}u}\left(\Gamma^{-1}_{v}x\right),\ \forall x\in P,\ u\in P_{k}.
\]
For any $x\in P$, we check 
\[
\sum_{u\in P_{k}}\lambda_{u}(x)=\sum_{v\in\mathrm{vert}F_{x}}\rho_{v}(x)\sum_{u\in P_{k}}B_{\Gamma^{-1}_{v}u}\left(\Gamma^{-1}_{v}x\right)=\sum_{v\in\mathrm{vert}F_{x}}\rho_{v}(x)=1,
\]
where $\sum_{u\in P_{k}}B_{\Gamma^{-1}_{v}u}\left(\Gamma^{-1}_{v}x\right)=1$
holds since (\ref{eq: field B}), $x\in\mathrm{relint}F_{x}$ and
$k$ is sufficiently large (depending on $\varepsilon$). Similarly,
we have 
\[
\sum_{u\in P_{k}}\lambda_{u}(x)u=x,\ \forall x\in P.
\]
Thus $\lambda$ is a coefficient field for $(P,P_{k})$. It yields the
upper bound (\ref{eq:lam give bound}). Next we give an upper bound
for $\int_{P}\lambda_{u}(x)$.

For a vertex $v$ and $u\in P_{k}$, changing the variables, we have
\begin{equation}
\int_{P}\rho_{v}(x)B_{\Gamma^{-1}_{v}u}\left(\Gamma^{-1}_{v}x\right)\mathrm{d}x=k^{-n}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\ge0}}\rho_{v}\left(\Gamma_{v}t\right)B_{\Gamma^{-1}_{v}u}(t)\mathrm{d}t,\label{eq: int rho}
\end{equation}
where we extend $\rho_{v}$ by zero to the entire cone $C_{v}$. Note
the support of $B_{\Gamma^{-1}_{v}u}(t)$ is 
\[
\left\{ t\in\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\ge0}\mid\left|t-\Gamma^{-1}_{v}u\right|_{\infty}\le1\right\} .
\]
Consider the Taylor expansion of $\rho_{v}\left(\Gamma_{v}t\right)$
near the point $\Gamma^{-1}_{v}u$, we have 
\[
\rho_{v}\left(\Gamma_{v}t\right)=\rho_{v}(u)+\frac{1}{k}\sum^{n}_{i=1}D_{e^{i}_{v}}\rho_{v}(u)\left(t_{i}-\left(\Gamma^{-1}_{v}u\right)_{i}\right)+R^{u}_{v}(t),
\]
where $\left|R^{u}_{v}(t)\right|\le Ck^{-2}\left|t-\Gamma^{-1}_{v}u\right|^{2}_{2}$
and $C$ depends on the $C^{2}$-norm of $\rho_{v}$. Bring this expansion
back to (\ref{eq: int rho}). Via direct computation, we have 
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\ge0}}B_{\Gamma^{-1}_{v}u}(t)\mathrm{d}t=2^{-\mathrm{cd}(u)},
\]
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}_{\ge0}}\left(t_{i}-\left(\Gamma^{-1}_{v}u\right)_{i}\right)B_{\Gamma^{-1}_{v}u}(t)\mathrm{d}t=\begin{cases}
2^{-\mathrm{cd}(u)}/3, & \left(\Gamma^{-1}_{v}u\right)_{i}=0,\\
0, & \left(\Gamma^{-1}_{v}u\right)_{i}>0.
\end{cases}
\]
Finally, we obtain upper bound, 
\[
k^{n}\int_{P}\lambda_{u}(x)\le2^{-\mathrm{cd}(u)}+\frac{C_{1}}{k}I_{\partial P}(u)+\frac{C_{2}}{k^{2}},
\]
where $C_{i}$ depends on the $C^{i}$-norm of $\{\rho_{v}\}$, and
$I_{\partial P}(u)$ is the indicator function of $\partial P$. Apply
this bound to (\ref{eq:lam give bound}), (\ref{eq:key estimate})
follows. 

Apply (\ref{eq:key estimate}) to each facet $F$, we obtain 
\[
k^{n-1}\int_{F}\phi\le\sum_{u\in F_{k}}2^{1-\mathrm{cd}(u)}\phi(u)+\frac{C^{F}_{1}}{k}\sum_{u\in\partial F\cap k^{-1}M}\phi(u)+\frac{C^{F}_{2}}{k^{2}}\sum_{u\in F_{k}}\phi(u).
\]
For Delzant polytopes, a boundary lattice point $u$ belongs to $\mathrm{cd}(u)$
facets. Take the sum over $F$, we obtain 
\[
k^{n-1}\int_{\partial P}\phi\le\sum_{u\in P_{k}\cap\partial P}\mathrm{cd}(u)\cdot2^{1-\mathrm{cd}(u)}\phi(u)+\frac{C^{\prime}_{1}}{k}\sum_{u\in\partial^{>1}P\cap k^{-1}M}\phi(u)+\frac{C^{\prime}_{2}}{k^{2}}\sum_{u\in P_{k}\cap\partial P}\phi(u),
\]
where $\partial^{>1}P$ is the union of faces with codimension $>1$.
Since $\mathrm{cd}(u)\cdot2^{1-\mathrm{cd}(u)}\le1$, (\ref{eq: b key estimate})
follows.

title: Proof
body_md:
If not, there exists a sequence of normalized convex functions $\phi_{k}$
so that 
\[
\left\Vert \phi_{k}\right\Vert _{k}=1,\text{ but }\left\Vert \phi_{k}-\pi_{k}\phi_{k}\right\Vert _{k}\rightarrow0.
\]
By (\ref{eq:rough bound}) and C-S inequality, $\int_{P}\phi_{k}$
is uniformly bounded. A compactness result \cite[Corollary 5.2.5]{donaldson_scalar_2002}
implies that, after passing to a subsequence, $\phi_{k}$ locally
uniformly converges to a normalized convex function $\phi$. 

Let $\alpha_{k}=\pi_{k}\phi_{k}$, we have $\left\Vert \alpha_{k}\right\Vert _{k}\le\left\Vert \phi_{k}\right\Vert _{k}=1$.
Since $\mathcal{A}$ is finite-dimensional, via a contradiction argument,
we can find a constant $C>0$ such that 
\begin{equation}
C^{-1}\left\Vert \alpha\right\Vert _{k}\le\sup_{P}\left|\alpha\right|\le C\left\Vert \alpha\right\Vert _{k},\ \forall\alpha\in\mathcal{A},\ k\ge1.\label{eq: finite dim norms}
\end{equation}
By the compactness in finite-dimensional spaces, we may assume $\alpha_{k}\rightarrow\alpha\in\mathcal{A}$. 

Let $\eta_{k}=\phi_{k}-\alpha_{k}$ and $\eta=\phi-\alpha$, so $\left\Vert \eta\right\Vert _{k}\rightarrow0$.
For any subpolytope $K\subset\mathrm{int}P$, by the uniform convergence
on $K$, we have 
\[
\frac{1}{k^{n}}\sum_{u\in P_{k}\cap K}\eta_{k}(u)^{2}-\frac{1}{k^{n}}\sum_{u\in P_{k}\cap K}\eta(u)^{2}\rightarrow0,\ \frac{1}{k^{n}}\sum_{u\in P_{k}\cap K}\eta(u)^{2}\rightarrow\int_{K}\eta^{2}.
\]
It implies 
\[
\int_{K}\eta^{2}=\lim_{k}\frac{1}{k^{n}}\sum_{u\in P_{k}\cap K}\eta_{k}(u)^{2}\le\lim_{k}\left\Vert \eta\right\Vert ^{2}_{k}=0
\]
for all $K$. Thus $\phi=\alpha$, and $\alpha=0$ since $\phi$ is
normalized. But this contradicts with 
\[
\int_{P}\alpha^{2}\leftarrow\left\Vert \alpha_{k}\right\Vert ^{2}_{k}=\left\Vert \phi_{k}\right\Vert ^{2}_{k}-\left\Vert \eta\right\Vert ^{2}_{k}\rightarrow1.
\]

Let $\beta_{k}=\sum^{n}_{i=1}c^{k}_{i}x_{i}+c^{k}_{0}$. Take $\alpha=1$
and $x_{j}$ ($1\le j\le n$) in (\ref{eq: def beta_k}), we obtain
a system of linear equations satisfying by $c^{k}_{i}$, 
\begin{align*}
\sum^{n}_{i=1}\left\langle 1,x_{i}\right\rangle _{k}c^{k}_{i}+\left\langle 1,1\right\rangle _{k}c^{k}_{0} & =L_{k}(1)\\
\sum^{n}_{i=1}\left\langle x_{j},x_{i}\right\rangle _{k}c^{k}_{i}+\left\langle x_{j},1\right\rangle _{k}c^{k}_{0} & =L_{k}(x_{j}),\ 1\le j\le n.
\end{align*}
By the expansion of Riemann sums, we have 
\[
\left\langle x_{j},x_{i}\right\rangle _{k}\rightarrow\int_{P}x_{j}x_{i},\ L_{k}(x_{j})\rightarrow\int_{\partial P}x_{j},\ \text{etc.}
\]
Since the coefficients of system tends to that of the system for $\ell_{P}$,
we have $\beta_{k}\rightarrow\ell_{P}$.

title: \protect\propositionname
body_md:
\label{prop: boundedness}Suppose $P$ is a Delzant lattice polytope,
then 
\[
\left\Vert \psi^{\perp}_{k}\right\Vert _{k},\ \left\Vert \phi_{k}\right\Vert _{k},\ \sup_{P}\left|\alpha_{k}\right|,\ \int_{\partial P}\phi_{k},\ \int_{P}\phi^{2}_{k}

label: eq:rel psi bound
title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\psi^{\perp}_{k}$ minimizes $\Psi^{\mathrm{rel}}_{k}$, we
have 
\begin{equation}
0=\Psi^{\mathrm{rel}}_{k}(0)\ge\Psi^{\mathrm{rel}}_{k}(\psi^{\perp}_{k})=\frac{1}{2}\left\Vert \psi^{\perp}_{k}\right\Vert ^{2}_{k}+L^{\mathrm{rel}}_{k}(\phi_{k}),\label{eq:rel psi bound}
\end{equation}
where we used the affine invariance of $L^{\mathrm{rel}}_{k}$. Employ
the fine estimate (\ref{eq:key estimate}), note that $1-2^{-\mathrm{cd}(u)}\ge\frac{1}{2}$
for $u\in P_{k}\cap\partial P$, we have 
\begin{align}
L_{k}(\phi_{k}) & \ge\frac{2}{k^{n-1}}\left(\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{C_{1}}{k}\right)\sum_{u\in P_{k}\cap\partial P}\phi_{k}(u)-\frac{C_{2}}{k^{2}}\sum_{u\in P_{k}}\phi_{k}(u)\right)\label{eq: estimate Lk}\\
\left(\text{suppose }\frac{C_{1}}{k}<\frac{1}{4}\right)\quad & \ge\frac{1}{2k^{n-1}}\sum_{u\in P_{k}\cap\partial P}\phi_{k}(u)-\frac{2C_{2}}{k^{n+1}}\sum_{u\in P_{k}}\phi_{k}(u)\nonumber \\
\text{C-S inequality}\quad & \ge\frac{1}{2k^{n-1}}\sum_{u\in P_{k}\cap\partial P}\phi_{k}(u)-\frac{C^{\prime}_{2}}{k}\left\Vert \phi_{k}\right\Vert _{k}.\nonumber 
\end{align}
Since $\beta_{k}\rightarrow\ell_{P}$, it is uniformly bounded, 
\[
\left|\left\langle \phi_{k},\beta_{k}\right\rangle _{k}\right|\le\frac{C_{\beta}}{k^{n}}\sum_{u\in P_{k}}\phi_{k}(u)\le C^{\prime}_{\beta}\left\Vert \phi_{k}\right\Vert _{k}.
\]
Bring these estimates to (\ref{eq:rel psi bound}), 
\[
0\ge\Psi^{\mathrm{rel}}_{k}(\psi^{\perp}_{k})=\frac{1}{2k^{n-1}}\sum_{u\in P_{k}\cap\partial P}\phi_{k}(u)+\frac{1}{2}\left\Vert \psi^{\perp}_{k}\right\Vert ^{2}_{k}-\left(C^{\prime}_{\beta}+\frac{C^{\prime}_{2}}{k}\right)\left\Vert \phi_{k}\right\Vert _{k}.
\]
Since $\phi_{k}-\pi_{k}\phi_{k}=\psi^{\perp}_{k}$, (\ref{eq:projection control})
gives 
\[
\left\Vert \phi_{k}\right\Vert _{k}\le C_{\pi}\left\Vert \psi^{\perp}_{k}\right\Vert _{k}.
\]
Since $\phi_{k}\ge0$, we obtain
\[
0\ge\frac{1}{2}\left\Vert \psi^{\perp}_{k}\right\Vert ^{2}_{k}-\left(C^{\prime}_{\beta}+\frac{C^{\prime}_{2}}{k}\right)C_{\pi}\left\Vert \psi^{\perp}_{k}\right\Vert _{k}.
\]
It implies the boundedness of $\left\Vert \psi^{\perp}_{k}\right\Vert _{k}$,
$\left\Vert \phi_{k}\right\Vert _{k}$ and $\frac{1}{k^{n-1}}\sum_{u\in P_{k}\cap\partial P}\phi_{k}(u).$
Then $\int_{\partial P}\phi_{k}\mathrm{d}\sigma$ is bounded since
(\ref{eq: b key estimate}). Since $\alpha_{k}=\psi^{\perp}_{k}-\phi_{k}$,
$\left\Vert \alpha_{k}\right\Vert _{k}$ is bounded, thus $\{\alpha_{k}\}$
are uniformly bounded by (\ref{eq: finite dim norms}). 

Finally, since $\phi_{k}\ge0$, $\phi^{2}_{k}$ is also convex. Employ
the rough estimate (\ref{eq:rough bound}), 
\[
\fint_{P}\phi^{2}_{k}\le C_{P}\left\Vert \phi_{k}\right\Vert ^{2}_{k}\le C.
\]

label: lem: little
title: \protect\lemmaname
body_md:
\label{lem: little}Let $P$ be a lattice polytope, $\psi_{k}\in C^{0}(P)$
locally uniformly converges to $\psi\in L^{1}(P)$ on $\mathrm{int}P$,
and $\left\Vert \psi_{k}\right\Vert _{k}\le C_{\psi}$ for all $k$.
Another sequence $\gamma_{k}\in C^{0}(P)$ uniformly converges to
$\gamma$. Then we have 
\[
\lim_{k}\left\langle \psi_{k},\gamma_{k}\right\rangle _{k}=\int_{P}\psi\gamma\mathrm{d}x.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose $\sup_{P}\left|\gamma_{k}\right|\le C_{\gamma}$ for all $k$.
For any $\varepsilon>0$, we can find a subpolytope $K\subset\mathrm{int}P$,
such that 
\[
2C_{\gamma}C_{\psi}\left|P\backslash K\right|^{1/2}<\varepsilon\text{ and }\left|\int_{P\backslash K}\psi\gamma\right|<\varepsilon.
\]
We have 
\[
\left|\left\langle \psi_{k},\gamma_{k}\right\rangle _{k}-\int_{P}\psi\gamma\right|\le\left|\frac{1}{k^{n}}\sum_{P_{k}\cap K}\psi_{k}\gamma_{k}-\int_{K}\psi\gamma\right|+\left|\frac{1}{k^{n}}\sum_{P_{k}\backslash K}\psi_{k}\gamma_{k}\right|+\left|\int_{P\backslash K}\psi\gamma\right|.
\]
The first term on the RHS tends to zero since $\psi_{k}\gamma_{k}\rightarrow\psi\gamma$
uniformly on $K$. By C-S inequality, 
\[
\text{middle term }\le C_{\gamma}\frac{\left|P_{k}\backslash K\right|^{1/2}}{k^{n/2}}\left\Vert \psi_{k}\right\Vert _{k}\le2C_{\gamma}C_{\psi}\left|P\backslash K\right|^{1/2}<\varepsilon.
\]
Hence there exists $N_{\varepsilon}>0$ such that the sum of three
terms is $<3\varepsilon$ for $k>N_{\varepsilon}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $\psi_{k}$ does not $L^{2}$-converge to $\psi$, then
there exists $\delta>0$ and a subsequence $\psi_{k_{j}}$ such that
\[
\left\Vert \psi_{k_{j}}-\psi\right\Vert _{L^{2}}\ge\delta,\ \forall j\ge1.
\]
We will show that $\psi_{k_{j}}$ admits a subsequence which $L^{2}$-converges
to $\psi$. It is a contradiction, we are done. For simplicity of
notation, we denote $\psi_{k_{j}}$ by $\psi_{k}$.

\textbf{Step 1}. Find the subsequence.

By Proposition \ref{prop: boundedness}, we have uniform boundedness,
\[
\left\Vert \phi_{k}\right\Vert _{k}+\sup_{P}\left|\alpha_{k}\right|+\int_{\partial P}\phi_{k}+\int_{P}\phi^{2}_{k}\le C.
\]
Using the weak compactness in $L^{2}(P)$ and Proposition \ref{prop: Donaldson compact},
we can take a subsequence (still denoted by $\psi_{k},\phi_{k}$)
such that 
\[
\phi_{k}\rightharpoonup\phi_{*}\text{ in }L^{2}(P),\ \phi_{k}\rightarrow\phi_{*}\text{ locally uniformly on }\mathrm{int}P,
\]
where $\phi_{*}\in\mathcal{C}_{1}(P)\cap L^{2}(P)$. Moreover, by
(\ref{eq: Donald liminf}) we have 
\begin{equation}
\liminf_{k}\int_{\partial P}\phi_{k}\ge\int_{\partial P}\phi_{*}.\label{eq: Donald liminf 2}
\end{equation}

Since $\alpha_{k}\in\mathcal{A}$ is also uniformly bounded, we can
assume $\alpha_{k}\rightarrow\alpha\in\mathcal{A}$ after passing to a subsequence.
Recall that 
\[
\psi_{k}=\psi^{\bot}_{k}-\beta_{k}=\phi_{k}+\alpha_{k}-\beta_{k}\text{ and }\beta_{k}\rightarrow\ell_{P},
\]
we have 
\[
\psi_{k}\rightharpoonup\psi_{*}\coloneqq\phi_{*}+\alpha-\ell_{P}\text{ in }L^{2}(P),\ \psi_{k}\rightarrow\psi_{*}\text{ locally uniformly on }\mathrm{int}P.
\]
Since $\left\Vert \psi_{k}\right\Vert _{k}$ is also bounded, we may
assume $\left\Vert \psi_{k}\right\Vert _{k}$ converges. We will not
take further subsequence in the following.

\textbf{Step 2}. show $\psi_{*}=\psi\coloneqq-\Theta_{P}$ and $\left\Vert \psi_{k}\right\Vert _{k}\rightarrow\left\Vert \psi\right\Vert _{L^{2}}$.

It suffices to show 
\begin{align}
\liminf_{k}\left\Vert \psi_{k}\right\Vert ^{2}_{k} & \ge\int_{P}\psi^{2}_{*},\text{ and }\label{eq: liminf L2 norm}\\
\liminf_{k}L_{k}(\psi_{k}) & \ge\int_{\partial P}\psi_{*}\mathrm{d}\sigma.\label{eq: liminf Lk}
\end{align}
Once these hold, since $\psi_{k}$ and $\psi$ are the minimizer of
$\Psi_{k}$ and $\Psi$ respectively, we have 
\begin{align*}
\Psi(\psi)=\lim_{k}\Psi_{k}(\psi) & \ge\limsup_{k}\Psi_{k}(\psi_{k})\ge\liminf_{k}\Psi_{k}(\psi_{k})\\
 & \ge\liminf_{k}\frac{1}{2}\left\Vert \psi_{k}\right\Vert ^{2}_{k}+\liminf_{k}L_{k}(\psi_{k})\\
 & \ge\frac{1}{2}\int_{P}\psi^{2}_{*}+\int_{\partial P}\psi_{*}\mathrm{d}\sigma=\Psi(\psi_{*})\ge\Psi(\psi),
\end{align*}
where the first equality is due to the continuity of $\Theta_{P}$
and (\ref{eq:EM}). All inequalities become equalities, thus 
\begin{equation}
\lim_{k}\Psi_{k}(\psi_{k})=\Psi(\psi)\text{ and }\Psi(\psi_{*})=\Psi(\psi).\label{eq:inf converge}
\end{equation}
The uniqueness of minimizer implies $\psi_{*}=\psi$. (\ref{eq: liminf L2 norm})
also takes equality, so 
\begin{equation}
\lim_{k}\left\Vert \psi_{k}\right\Vert _{k}=\left\Vert \psi\right\Vert _{L^{2}},\label{eq: normk converge}
\end{equation}
since we know that $\left\Vert \psi_{k}\right\Vert _{k}$ converges
in Step1. 

To prove (\ref{eq: liminf L2 norm}), take any compact $K\subset\mathrm{int}P$,
by uniform convergence, 
\[
\liminf_{k}\left\Vert \psi_{k}\right\Vert ^{2}_{k}\ge\lim_{k}\frac{1}{k^{n}}\sum_{u\in P_{k}\cap K}\psi_{k}(u)^{2}=\int_{K}\psi^{2}_{*}.
\]
Take the supremum over $K$, (\ref{eq: liminf L2 norm}) follows.

For (\ref{eq: liminf Lk}), combine the estimate (\ref{eq: estimate Lk})
and (\ref{eq: b key estimate}), we have 
\begin{align}
L_{k}(\phi_{k}) & \ge\left(1-\frac{2C_{1}}{k}\right)\frac{1}{k^{n-1}}\sum_{u\in P_{k}\cap\partial P}\phi_{k}(u)-\frac{2C_{2}}{k^{n+1}}\sum_{u\in P_{k}}\phi_{k}(u)\label{eq:key usage}\\
 & \ge\left(1-\frac{2C_{1}}{k}\right)\left(1+\frac{C_{b}}{k}\right)^{-1}\int_{\partial P}\phi_{k}\mathrm{d}\sigma-\frac{2C_{2}}{k^{n+1}}\sum_{u\in P_{k}}\phi_{k}(u).\nonumber 
\end{align}
The last term tends to zero since $\left\Vert \phi_{k}\right\Vert _{k}\le C$.
Take $\liminf_{k}$ on both sides, use (\ref{eq: Donald liminf 2}),
we obtain 
\[
\liminf_{k}L_{k}(\phi_{k})\ge\int_{\partial P}\phi_{*}\mathrm{d}\sigma.
\]
This implies (\ref{eq: liminf Lk}) since $\alpha_{k}\rightarrow\alpha$ and
$\beta_{k}\rightarrow\ell_{P}$ uniformly.

\textbf{Step 3}. Show the subsequence $\psi_{k}\xrightarrow{L^{2}}\psi$.

Since $\phi^{2}_{k}$ is also convex, apply (\ref{eq:key estimate}),
\[
\int_{P}\phi^{2}_{k}\le\frac{1}{k^{n}}\sum_{u\in P_{k}}\phi_{k}(u)^{2}+\frac{C_{1}}{k^{n+1}}\sum_{u\in P_{k}\cap\partial P}\phi_{k}(u)^{2}+\frac{C_{2}}{k^{n+2}}\sum_{u\in P_{k}}\phi_{k}(u)^{2}
\]
The last two terms tends to zero since $\left\Vert \phi_{k}\right\Vert _{k}\le C$.
Take $\limsup$ on both sides, 
\[
\limsup_{k}\int_{P}\phi^{2}_{k}\le\limsup_{k}\left\Vert \phi_{k}\right\Vert ^{2}_{k}.
\]
We show the RHS is $\int_{P}\phi^{2}_{*}$. Write $\psi_{k}=\phi_{k}+\gamma_{k}$,
where $\gamma_{k}\coloneqq\alpha_{k}-\beta_{k}\rightarrow\gamma\coloneqq\alpha-\ell_{P}$.
Use (\ref{eq: normk converge}) and Lemma \ref{lem: little}, 
\[
\left\Vert \phi_{k}\right\Vert ^{2}_{k}=\left\Vert \psi_{k}\right\Vert ^{2}_{k}-2\left\langle \psi_{k},\gamma_{k}\right\rangle +\left\Vert \gamma_{k}\right\Vert ^{2}_{k}\rightarrow\left\Vert \psi\right\Vert ^{2}_{L^{2}}-2\int_{P}\psi\gamma+\int_{P}\gamma^{2}=\int_{P}\phi^{2}_{*}.
\]
Hence $\limsup\int_{P}\phi^{2}_{k}\le\int_{P}\phi^{2}_{*}$. Lower
semicontinuity of $L^{2}$-norm (for weak convergence) gives the converse
direction: $\liminf\int_{P}\phi^{2}_{k}\ge\int_{P}\phi^{2}_{*}$.
Hence we have 
\[
\lim_{k}\left\Vert \phi_{k}\right\Vert _{L^{2}}=\left\Vert \phi_{*}\right\Vert _{L^{2}}.
\]
This implies $\phi_{k}\xrightarrow{L^{2}}\phi_{*}$ since we already
have $\phi_{k}\rightharpoonup\phi_{*}$. So 
\[
\psi_{k}=\phi_{k}+\gamma_{k}\xrightarrow{L^{2}}\phi_{*}+\gamma=\psi.
\]
This is just the $L^{2}$-convergence of the subsequence selected
in Step 1. As stated at the beginning of the proof, by a contradiction
argument, we can obtain the $L^{2}$-convergence of the full sequence.
By (\ref{eq:inf converge}), we also have $\lim_{k}\Psi_{k}(\psi_{k})=\Psi(\psi)$. 

For the locally uniformly convergence, if there is a compact set $K\subset\mathrm{int}P$
such that $\sup_{K}\left|\psi_{k}-\psi\right|\not\rightarrow0$. By
the above argument, we can find a subsequence which locally uniformly
converges to $\psi$. It is a contradiction.

Finally, we show $\mathbb{M}^{\mathrm{rel}}_{P}(\psi_{k})\rightarrow\mathbb{M}^{\mathrm{rel}}_{P}(\psi)$.
Since $\psi_{k}\xrightarrow{L^{2}}\psi$, it suffices to show $\int_{\partial P}\psi_{k}\rightarrow\int_{\partial P}\psi$.
For any subsequence $\psi_{k_{j}}$, we show it admits a further subsequence
so that its boundary integral converges to $\int_{\partial P}\psi$.
Then we are done. 

Choose a subsequence as in Step 1 above, and still denote it by $\psi_{k}$.
We can use all the results obtained in Step 2 and 3. Combine $\lim\Psi_{k}(\psi_{k})=\Psi(\psi)$
with (\ref{eq: normk converge}), we have $\lim L_{k}(\psi_{k})=\int_{\partial P}\psi$.
Recall $\psi_{k}=\phi_{k}+\gamma_{k}$ and $\gamma_{k}\rightrightarrows\gamma$,
it follows that 
\[
\lim_{k}L_{k}(\phi_{k})=\int_{\partial P}\phi_{*},\  \phi_{*}=\psi-\gamma.
\]
Take $\limsup_{k}$ on both sides of (\ref{eq:key usage}), we obtain
\[
\int_{\partial P}\phi_{*}=\lim_{k}L_{k}(\phi_{k})\ge\limsup_{k}\int_{\partial P}\phi_{k}.
\]
(\ref{eq: Donald liminf 2}) gives the reverse side, hence $\int_{\partial P}\phi_{k}\rightarrow\int_{\partial P}\phi_{*}$.
This implies $\int_{\partial P}\psi_{k}\rightarrow\int_{\partial P}\psi$
since $\gamma_{k}\rightrightarrows\gamma$.

label: rem: fail nonDelzant
title: \protect\remarkname
body_md:
\label{rem: fail nonDelzant}The most delicate step in the proof is
(\ref{eq:key usage}). It requires an estimate of the form: 
\[
k^{n}\int_{P}\phi\le\sum_{u\in P_{k}}w(u)\phi(u)+\frac{C_{1}}{k}\sum_{u\in P_{k}\cap\partial P}\phi(u)+\frac{C_{2}}{k^{2}}\sum_{u\in P_{k}}\phi(u)
\]
holds for all convex $\phi\ge0$, and the weight $w(u)$ satisfies
\[
\begin{cases}
w(u)=1, & u\in\mathrm{int}P,\\
w(u)=1/2, & \mathrm{cd}(u)=1,\\
w(u)\le1/2, & \mathrm{cd}(u)>1.
\end{cases}
\]
Such estimate may not exist for non-Delzant polytope, for instance
\[
P=\mathrm{conv}\left((0,0),(1,0),(1,m)\right),\ m\ge4,
\]
which is singular at the vertex $(0,0)$. We take $\phi=\max\left\{ 1-kx_{1},0\right\} $
and compute 
\[
k^{2}\int_{P}\phi=\frac{m}{6}\text{ and }\phi(u)=0,\ \forall u\in P_{k}\backslash\{(0,0)\}.
\]
The above inequality implies 
\[
\frac{2}{3}\le\frac{m}{6}\le w(0,0)+\frac{C_{1}}{k}+\frac{C_{2}}{k^{2}}.
\]
Since $w(0,0)\le1/2$, for any $C_{1},C_{2}$, we can find a sufficiently
large $k$ making this inequality fail.

title: Proof
body_md:
This is also a typical $\Gamma$-convergence argument as the Step
2 above, but we use $C^{0}$-topology. In the following, convergence
always means the uniform convergence on $P$.

We assume that $\{\psi_{k}\}$ is $C^{0}$-precompact. Since $\Psi_{k}(\psi)\ge\Psi_{k}(\psi_{k})$,
we have 
\[
\Psi(\psi)=\lim_{k}\Psi_{k}(\psi)\ge\limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty}\Psi_{k}(\psi_{k}),
\]
where the first equality is due to the continuity of $\Theta_{P}$
and (\ref{eq:EM}).

If one can show that each subsequence of $\psi_{k}$ has a further
subsequence which uniformly converges to $\psi$, then by a contradiction
argument, we obtain $\psi_{k}\rightarrow\psi$ uniformly. Without loss of
generality, we only consider the sequence $\psi_{k}$ itself.

By the precompactness assumption, $\psi_{k}$ has a subsequence $\psi_{k_{j}}$
which uniformly converges to $\psi_{*}\in\mathcal{C}(P)$. It remains
to show $\psi_{*}=\psi$. Apply (\ref{eq:EM enhanced}), we have 
\[
\liminf_{j\rightarrow\infty}\Psi_{k_{j}}(\psi_{k_{j}})=\Psi(\psi_{*})\geq\Psi(\psi).
\]
We already have $\Psi(\psi)\ge\limsup_{j}\Psi_{k_{j}}(\psi_{k_{j}})$.
It forces $\Psi(\psi_{*})=\Psi(\psi)$, so $\psi_{*}=\psi$ by the
uniqueness of minimizer.

(1) when $f$ is smooth on an open set containing $P$, (\ref{eq:EM})
is just the leading two terms of the Euler--Maclaurin expansion.
There is vast literature discussing it, see \cite{tate_asymptotic_2011}
and its references. (2) if $f$ is merely continuous, (\ref{eq:EM})
may fail even in one dimension (Weierstrass type functions). (3) If
$f$ is convex and piece-wisely linear with rational coefficients,
(\ref{eq:EM}) can be derived from the asymptotics of lattice point
counting, see \cite[Prop. 4.1.3]{donaldson_scalar_2002}. In our setting,
(\ref{eq:EM}) cannot be derived from these results via a direct approximation.
The key in the following proof is decomposing the Riemann sum into
interior part and boundary part, and we handle the boundary part via
approximation.
